⟦b:sē amāre⟧, ⟦i:to love one's self⟧;
⟦b:suum genium propitiāre⟧, ⟦i:to propitiate one's own genius⟧.
4. ⟦b:Suus⟧ sometimes occurs in the meaning ⟦i:his own⟧, ⟦i:their own⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧, referring not to the subject but to an oblique case; as,—
⟦b:Hannibalem suī cīvēs ē cīvitāte ējēcērunt⟧, ⟦i:his own fellow-citizens drove out Hannibal.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. This usage is particularly frequent in combination with ⟦b:quisque⟧; as,—
⟦b:suus quemque error vexat⟧, ⟦i:his own error troubles each⟧.
5. The Reflexives for the first and second persons are supplied by the oblique cases of ⟦b:ego⟧ and ⟦b:tū⟧ (§ 85); as,—
⟦b:vōs dēfenditis⟧, ⟦i:you defend yourselves⟧.

title: Reciprocal Pronouns
Syntax of demonstrative pronouns
text:
1. Where ⟦b:hīc⟧ and ⟦b:ille⟧ are used in contrast, ⟦b:hīc⟧ usually refers to the latter of two objects, and ⟦b:ille⟧ to the former.
2. ⟦b:Hīc⟧ and ⟦b:ille⟧ are often used in the sense of 'the following'; as,—
⟦b:Themistoclēs hīs verbīs epistulam mīsit⟧, ⟦i:Themistocles sent a letter (couched) in the following words⟧;
⟦b:illud intellegō, omnium ōra in mē conversa esse⟧, ⟦i:I understand this, that the faces of all are turned toward me⟧.
3. ⟦b:Ille⟧ often means ⟦i:the famous⟧; as, ⟦b:Solōn ille⟧, ⟦i:the famous Solon⟧.
4. ⟦b:Iste⟧ frequently involves contempt; as, ⟦b:iste homō⟧, ⟦i:that fellow!⟧
5. The above pronouns, along with ⟦b:is⟧, are usually attracted to the gender of a predicate noun; as, ⟦b:hīc est honor, meminisse officium suum⟧, ⟦i:this is an honor, to be mindful of one's duty.⟧
Is.
1. ⟦b:Is⟧ often serves as the antecedent of the relative ⟦b:quī⟧. Thus:—
⟦b:Maximum, eum quī Tarentum recēpit, dīlēxī⟧, ⟦i:I loved Maximus, the man who retook Tarentum⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Closely akin to this usage is ⟦b:is⟧ in the sense of ⟦i:such⟧ (= ⟦b:tālis⟧); as,—
⟦b:nōn sum is quī terrear⟧, ⟦i:I am not such a person as to be frightened⟧.
⟦i:b⟧. Note the phrase ⟦b:id quod⟧, where ⟦b:id⟧ stands in apposition with an entire clause; as,—
⟦b:nōn suspicābātur (id quod nunc sentiet) satis multōs testēs nōbīs reliquōs esse⟧, ⟦i:he did not suspect (a thing which he will now perceive) that we had witnesses enough left⟧.
Yet ⟦b:quod⟧ alone, without preceding ⟦b:id⟧, sometimes occurs in this use.
2. ⟦b:Is⟧ also in all cases serves as the personal pronoun of the third person, '⟦i:he⟧,' '⟦i:she⟧,' '⟦i:it⟧,' '⟦i:they⟧,' '⟦i:them⟧.'
3. When the English uses '⟦i:that of⟧,' '⟦i:those of⟧,' to avoid repetition of the noun, the Latin omits the pronoun: as,—
⟦b:in exercitū Sullae et posteā in Crassī fuerat⟧, ⟦i:he had been in the army of Sulla and afterward in that of Crassus⟧;
⟦b:nūllae mē fābulae dēlectant nisi Plautī⟧, ⟦i:no plays delight me except those of Plautus⟧.
4. Note the phrases ⟦b:et is⟧, ⟦b:et ea⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧, in the sense: ⟦i:and that too⟧; as,—
⟦b:vincula, et ea sempiterna⟧, ⟦i:imprisonment, and that too permanently⟧.
Īdem.
1. ⟦b:Īdem⟧ in apposition with the subject or object often has the force of ⟦i:also⟧, ⟦i:likewise⟧; as,—
⟦b:quod idem mihi contigit⟧, ⟦i:which likewise happened to me⟧ (lit. ⟦i:which, the same thing⟧);
⟦b:bonus vir, quem eundem sapientem appellāmus⟧, ⟦i:a good man, whom we call also wise⟧.
For ⟦b:īdem atque (ac)⟧, ⟦i:the same as⟧, see § 341, 1. ⟦i:c⟧.
Ipse.
1. ⟦b:Ipse⟧, literally ⟦i:self⟧, acquires its special force from the context; as,—
⟦b:eō ipsō diē⟧, ⟦i:on that very day⟧;
⟦b:ad ipsam rīpam⟧, ⟦i:close to the bank⟧;
⟦b:ipsō terrōre⟧, ⟦i:by mere fright⟧;
⟦b:valvae sē ipsae aperuērunt⟧, ⟦i:the doors opened of their own accord⟧;
⟦b:ipse aderat⟧, ⟦i:he was present in person⟧.
2. The reflexive pronouns are often emphasized by the addition of ⟦b:ipse⟧, but ipse in such cases, instead of standing in apposition with the reflexive, more commonly agrees with the subject; as,—
⟦b:sēcum ipsī loquuntur⟧, ⟦i:they talk with themselves⟧;
⟦b:sē ipse continēre nōn potest⟧, ⟦i:he cannot contain himself⟧
3. ⟦b:Ipse⟧ is also used as an Indirect Reflexive for the purpose of ⟦i:marking a contrast or avoiding an ambiguity⟧; as,—
⟦b:Persae pertimuērunt nē Alcibiadēs ab ipsīs dēscīsceret et cum suīs in grātiam redīret⟧, ⟦i:the Persians feared that Alcibiades would break with them and become reconciled with his countrymen⟧;
⟦b:ea molestissimē ferre dēbent hominēs quae ipsōrum culpā contrācta sunt⟧, ⟦i:men ought to chafe most over those things which have been brought about by their own fault⟧ (as opposed to the fault of others).

title: Syntax of relative pronouns
text:
⟦b:Agreement.⟧ 1. The Relative Pronoun agrees with its antecedent in Gender, Number, and Person, but its case is determined by its construction in the clause in which it stands; as,—
⟦b:mulier quam vidēbāmus⟧, ⟦i:the woman whom we saw⟧;
⟦b:bona quibus fruimur⟧, ⟦i:the blessings which we enjoy⟧.
2. Where the antecedent is compound, the same principles for number and gender prevail as in case of predicate adjectives under similar conditions (see § 235, ⟦i:B⟧, 2). Thus:—
⟦b:pater et fīlius, qui captī sunt⟧, ⟦i:the father and son who were captured⟧;
⟦b:stultitia et timiditās quae fugienda sunt⟧, ⟦i:folly and cowardice which must be shunned⟧;
⟦b:honōrēs et victōriae quae sunt fortuīta⟧, ⟦i:honors and victories, which are accidental⟧.
3. The Relative regularly agrees with a predicate noun (either Nominative or Accusative) instead of its antecedent; as,—
⟦b:carcer, quae lautumiae vocantur⟧, ⟦i:the prison, which is called Lautumiae⟧;
⟦b:Belgae, quae est tertia pars⟧, ⟦i:the Belgians, who are the third part⟧.
4. Sometimes the Relative takes its gender and number from the meaning of its antecedent; as,—
⟦b:pars quī bēstiīs objectī sunt⟧, ⟦i:a part (of the men) who were thrown to beasts.⟧
5. Occasionally the Relative is attracted into the case of its antecedent; as,—
⟦b:nātus eō patre quō dīxī⟧, ⟦i:born of the father that I said⟧.
⟦b:Antecedent⟧. 1. The antecedent of the Relative is sometimes omitted; as,—
⟦b:quī nātūram sequitur sapiēns est⟧, ⟦i:he who follows Nature is wise⟧.
2. The antecedent may be implied in a possessive pronoun (or rarely an adjective); as,—
⟦b:nostra quī remānsimus caedēs⟧, ⟦i:the slaughter of us who remained⟧;
⟦b:servīlī tumultū, quōs ūsus ac disciplīna sublevārunt⟧, ⟦i:at the uprising of the slaves, whom experience and discipline assisted⟧ (⟦b:servīlī = servōrum⟧).
3. Sometimes the antecedent is repeated with the Relative; as,—
⟦b:erant itinera duo, quibus itineribus⟧, ⟦i:there were two routes, by which (routes).⟧
4. Incorporation of Antecedent in Relative Clause. The antecedent is often incorporated in the relative clause. Thus:—
⟦i:a⟧) When the relative clause stands first; as,—
⟦b:quam quisque nōvit artem, in hāc sē exerceat⟧, ⟦i:let each one practice the branch which he knows.⟧
⟦i:b⟧) When the antecedent is an appositive; as,—
⟦b:nōn longē ā Tolōsātium fīnibus absunt, quae cīvitās est in prōvinciā⟧, ⟦i:they are not far from the borders of the Tolosates, a state which is in our province.⟧
⟦i:c⟧) When the logical antecedent is a superlative; as,—
⟦b:Themistoclēs dē servīs suīs, quem habuit fidēlissimum, mīsit⟧, ⟦i:Themistocles sent the most trusty slave he had⟧.
⟦i:d⟧) In expressions of the following type—
⟦b:quā es prūdentiā; quae tua est prūdentia⟧, ⟦i:such is your prudence⟧ (lit. ⟦i:of which prudence you are; which is your prudence⟧).
5. The Relative is never omitted in Latin as it is in English. Thus ⟦i:the boy I saw⟧ must be ⟦b:puer quem vīdī⟧.
6. The Relative is used freely in Latin, particularly at the beginning of a sentence, where in English we employ a demonstrative; as,—
⟦b:quō factum est⟧, ⟦i:by this it happened⟧;
⟦b:quae cum ita sint⟧, ⟦i:since this is so⟧;
⟦b:quibus rēbus cognitīs⟧, ⟦i:when these things became known⟧.
7. The Relative introducing a subordinate clause may belong grammatically to a clause which is subordinate to the one it introduces; as,—
⟦b:numquam dignē satis laudārī philosophia poterit, cui quī pāreat, omne tempus aetātis sine molestiā possit dēgere⟧, ⟦i:philosophy can never be praised enough, since he who obeys her can pass every period of life without annoyance⟧ (lit. ⟦i:he who obeys which, etc.⟧).
Here ⟦b:cui⟧ introduces the subordinate clause ⟦b:possit⟧ and connects it with ⟦b:philosophia⟧; but ⟦b:cui⟧ is governed by ⟦b:pāreat⟧, which is subordinate to ⟦b:possit⟧.

title: Syntax of indefinite pronouns
text:
1. ⟦b:Quis⟧, ⟦i:any one⟧, is the weakest of the Indefinites, and stands usually in combination with ⟦b:sī⟧, ⟦b:nisi⟧, ⟦b:nē⟧, ⟦b:num⟧; as,—
⟦b:sī quis putat⟧, ⟦i:if any one thinks⟧.
2. ⟦b:Aliquis⟧ (adj. ⟦b:aliquī⟧) is more definite than ⟦b:quis⟧, and corresponds usually to the English ⟦i:some one⟧, ⟦i:somebody⟧, ⟦i:some⟧; as,—
⟦b:nunc aliquis dīcat mihī⟧, ⟦i:now let somebody tell me⟧;
⟦b:utinam modo agātur aliquid⟧, ⟦i:oh that something may be done⟧.
3. ⟦b:Quīdam⟧, ⟦i:a certain one⟧, is still more definite than ⟦b:aliquis⟧; as,—
⟦b:homō quīdam⟧, ⟦i:a certain man⟧ (⟦i:i.e.⟧, ⟦i:one whom I have in mind⟧).
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Quīdam⟧ (with or without ⟦b:quasi⟧, ⟦i:as if⟧) is sometimes used in the sense: ⟦i:a sort of⟧, ⟦i:kind of;⟧ as,—
⟦b:cognātiō quaedam⟧, ⟦i:a sort of relationship⟧;
⟦b:mors est quasi quaedam migrātiō⟧, ⟦i:death is a kind of transfer as it were⟧.
4. ⟦b:Quisquam⟧, ⟦i:any one⟧, ⟦i:any one whoever⟧ (more general than ⟦b:quis⟧), and its corresponding adjective ⟦b:ūllus⟧, ⟦i:any⟧, occur mostly in negative and conditional sentences, in interrogative sentences implying a negative, and in clauses of comparison; as,—
⟦b:jūstitia numquam nocet cuiquam⟧, ⟦i:justice never harms anybody⟧;
⟦b:sī quisquam, Catō sapiēns fuit⟧, ⟦i:if anybody was ever wise, Cato was⟧;
⟦b:potestne quisquam sine perturbātiōne animī īrāscī⟧, ⟦i:can anybody be angry without excitement?⟧
⟦b:sī ūllō modō poterit⟧, ⟦i:if it can be done in any way⟧;
⟦b:taetrior hīc tyrannus fuit quam quisquam superiōrum⟧, ⟦i:he was a viler tyrant than any of his predecessors⟧.
5. ⟦b:Quisque⟧, ⟦i:each one⟧, is used especially under the following circumstances:—
⟦i:a⟧) In connection with ⟦b:suus⟧. See § 244, 4, ⟦i:a⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) In connection with a Relative or Interrogative Pronoun; as,—
⟦b:quod cuique obtigit, id teneat⟧, ⟦i:what falls to each, that let him hold⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) In connection with superlatives; as,—
⟦b:optimus quisque⟧, ⟦i:all the best⟧ (lit. ⟦i:each best one⟧).
⟦i:d⟧) With ordinal numerals; as,—
⟦b:quīntō quōque annō⟧, ⟦i:every four years⟧ (lit. ⟦i:each fifth year⟧).
6. ⟦b:Nēmō⟧, ⟦i:no one⟧, in addition to its other uses, stands regularly with adjectives used substantively; as,—
⟦b:nēmō mortālis⟧, ⟦i:no mortal⟧;
⟦b:nēmō Rōmānus⟧, ⟦i:no Roman⟧.

title: Syntax of pronominal adjectives
text:
1. ⟦b:Alius⟧, ⟦i:another⟧, and ⟦b:alter⟧, ⟦i:the other⟧, are often used correlatively; as,—
⟦b:aliud loquitur, aliud sentit⟧, ⟦i:he says one thing, he thinks another⟧;
⟦b:aliī resistunt, aliī fugiunt⟧, ⟦i:some resist, others flee⟧;
⟦b:alter exercitum perdidit, alter vēndidit⟧, ⟦i:one ruined the army, the other sold it⟧;
⟦b:alterī sē in montem recēpērunt, alterī ad impedīmenta sē contulērunt⟧, ⟦i:the one party retreated to the mountain, the others betook themselves to the baggage⟧.
2. Where the English says ⟦i:one does one thing, another another⟧, the Latin uses a more condensed form of statement; as,—
⟦b:alius aliud amat⟧, ⟦i:one likes one thing, another another⟧;
⟦b:aliud aliīs placet⟧, ⟦i:one thing pleases some, another others⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. So sometimes with adverbs; as,—
⟦b:aliī aliō fugiunt⟧, ⟦i:some flee in one direction, others in another⟧.
3. The Latin also expresses the notion '⟦i:each other⟧' by means of ⟦b:alius⟧ repeated; as,—
⟦b:Gallī alius alium cohortātī sunt⟧, ⟦i:the Gauls encouraged each other⟧.
4. ⟦b:Cēterī⟧ means ⟦i:the rest⟧, ⟦i:all the others⟧; as,—
⟦b:cēterīs praestāre⟧, ⟦i:to be superior to all the others⟧.
5. ⟦b:Reliquī⟧ means ⟦i:the others⟧ in the sense of ⟦i:the rest⟧, ⟦i:those remaining⟧,—hence is the regular word with numerals; as,—
⟦b:reliquī sex⟧, ⟦i:the six others⟧.
6. ⟦b:Nescio quis⟧ forms a compound indefinite pronoun with the force of ⟦i:some one or other⟧; as,—
⟦b:causidicus nescio quis⟧, ⟦i:some pettifogger or other⟧;
⟦b:mīsit nescio quem⟧, ⟦i:he sent some one or other⟧;
⟦b:nescio quō pactō⟧, ⟦i:somehow or other⟧.
With One Subject.

title: Agreement
text:
1. ⟦b:Agreement in Number and Person⟧. A Finite Verb agrees with its subject in Number and Person; as,—
⟦b:vōs vidētis⟧, ⟦i:you see⟧;
⟦b:pater fīliōs īnstituit⟧, ⟦i:the father trains his sons⟧.
2. ⟦b:Agreement in Gender⟧. In the compound forms of the verb the participle regularly agrees with its subject in gender; as,—
⟦b:sēditiō repressa est⟧, ⟦i:the mutiny was checked⟧.
3. But when a predicate noun is of different gender or number from its subject, the verb usually agrees with its nearest substantive; as,—
⟦b:Tarquiniī māterna patria erat⟧, ⟦i:Tarquinii was his native country on his mother's side⟧;
⟦b:nōn omnis error stultitia est dīcenda⟧, ⟦i:not every error is to be called folly⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Less frequently the verb agrees with an appositive; as,—
⟦b:Coriolī, oppidum Volscōrum, captum est⟧, ⟦i:Corioli, a town of the Volsci, was captured⟧.
4. ⟦b:Construction according to Sense⟧. Sometimes the verb agrees with its subject according to sense instead of strict grammatical form. Thus:—
⟦i:a⟧) In Number; as,—
⟦b:multitūdō hominum convēnerant⟧, ⟦i:a crowd of men had gathered⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) In Gender; as,—
⟦b:duo mīlia crucibus adfīxī sunt⟧, ⟦i:two thousand (men) were crucified⟧.
With Two or More Subjects.
1. ⟦b:Agreement in Number⟧. With two or more subjects the verb is regularly plural; as,—
⟦b:pater et fīlius mortuī sunt⟧, ⟦i:the father and son died⟧.
2. But sometimes the verb agrees with the nearest subject; ⟦i:viz.⟧,—
⟦i:a⟧) When the verb precedes both subjects or stands between them; as,—
⟦b:mortuus est pater et fīlius⟧;
⟦b:pater mortuus est et fīlius⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) When the subjects are connected by ⟦b:aut⟧; ⟦b:aut ... aut⟧; ⟦b:vel ... vel⟧; ⟦b:neque ... neque⟧; as,—
⟦b:neque pater neque fīlius mortuus est⟧, ⟦i:neither father nor son died⟧.
3. When the different subjects are felt together as constituting a whole, the singular is used; as,—
⟦b:temeritās ignōrātiōque vitiōsa est⟧, ⟦i:rashness and ignorance are bad⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. This is regularly the case in ⟦b:senātus populusque Rōmānus⟧.
4. ⟦b:Agreement in Person⟧. With compound subjects of different persons the verb always takes the ⟦i:first⟧ person rather than the ⟦i:second⟧, and the ⟦i:second⟧ rather than the ⟦i:third⟧; as,—
⟦b:sī tū et Tullia valētis, ego et Cicerō valēmus⟧, ⟦i:if you and Tullia are well, Cicero and I are well⟧.
5. ⟦b:Agreement in Gender⟧. With subjects of different genders the participle in the compound tenses follows the same principles as laid down for predicate adjectives. See § 235, ⟦i:B⟧, 2.

title: Voices
text:
1. The Passive Voice sometimes retains traces of its original middle or reflexive meaning; as,—
⟦b:ego nōn patiar eum dēfendī⟧, ⟦i:I shall not allow him to defend himself⟧.
2. In imitation of Greek usage many perfect passive participles are used by the poets as indirect middles, ⟦i:i.e.⟧ the subject is viewed as acting not upon itself, but as doing something ⟦i:in his own interest⟧; as,—
⟦b:vēlātus tempora⟧, ⟦i:having veiled his temples⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Occasionally finite forms of the verb are thus used; as,—
⟦b:tunicā indūcitur artūs⟧, ⟦i:he covers his limbs with a tunic⟧.
3. Intransitive Verbs may be used impersonally in the passive; as,—
⟦b:curritur⟧, ⟦i:people run⟧ (lit. ⟦i:it is run⟧);
⟦b:ventum est⟧, ⟦i:he⟧ (⟦i:they⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧) ⟦i:came⟧ (lit. ⟦i:it was come⟧).

title: Tenses of the Indicative
text:
1. The Latin tenses express two distinct notions:—
⟦i:a⟧) The ⟦i:period of time⟧ to which the action belongs: Present, Past, or Future.
⟦i:b⟧) The ⟦i:kind of action⟧: Undefined, Going on, or Completed.
The Latin with its six tenses is able to express each of the three kinds of action for each of the three periods of time (making practically nine tenses). It does this by employing certain tenses in more than one way, as may be seen by the following table:—
KIND OF ACTION.  PERIOD OF TIME.
⟦.⟧  PRESENT.  PAST.  FUTURE.
UNDEFINED  Present: ⟦b:scrībō⟧, ⟦i:I write⟧.  Historical Perfect: ⟦b:scrīpsī⟧, ⟦i:I wrote⟧.  Future: ⟦b:scrībam⟧, ⟦i:I shall write⟧.
GOING ON.  Present: ⟦b:scrībō⟧, ⟦i:I am writing⟧.  Imperfect: ⟦b:scrībēbam⟧, ⟦i:I was writing⟧.  Future: ⟦b:scrībam⟧, ⟦i:I shall be writing⟧.
COMPLETED.  Present Perfect: ⟦b:scrīpsī⟧, ⟦i:I have written⟧.  Pluperfect: ⟦b:scrīpseram⟧, ⟦i:I had written⟧.  Future Perfect: ⟦b:scrīpserō⟧, ⟦i:I shall have written⟧.
⟦/⟧
2. It will be seen that the Present may express Undefined action or action Going on; so also the Future. The Perfect likewise has a double use, according as it denotes action Completed in present time (Present Perfect) or Undefined action belonging to past time (Historical Perfect).
Principal and Historical Tenses.
Tenses which denote Present or Future time are called ⟦b:Principal⟧ (or Primary) Tenses, those which denote Past time are called ⟦b:Historical⟧ (or Secondary).
The Principal Tenses of the Indicative are: Present, Future, Present Perfect, Future Perfect.
The Historical Tenses are: Imperfect, Historical Perfect, Pluperfect.
Present Indicative.
Besides the two uses indicated in the table, the Present Indicative presents the following peculiarities:—
1. It is used to denote ⟦i:a general truth⟧, ⟦i:i.e.⟧ something true not merely in the present but at all times ('Gnomic Present'); as,—
⟦b:virtūs conciliat amīcitiās et cōnservat⟧, ⟦i:virtue establishes ties of friendship and maintains them⟧ (⟦i:i.e.⟧ always does so).
2. It is used of an attempted action ('Conative Present'); as,—
⟦b:dum vītant vitia, in contrāria currunt⟧, ⟦i:while they try to avoid⟧ (⟦b:vītant⟧) ⟦i:vices, they rush into opposite ones⟧.
3. In lively narration the Present is often used of a past action ('Historical Present'); as,—
⟦b:Caesar imperat magnum numerum obsidum⟧, ⟦i:Caesar demanded a large number of hostages⟧ (lit. ⟦i:demands⟧).
4. In combination with ⟦b:jam⟧, ⟦b:jam diū⟧, ⟦b:jam prīdem⟧, and similar words, the Present is frequently used of an action originating in the past and continuing in the present; as,—
⟦b:jam prīdem cupiō tē vīsere⟧, ⟦i:I have long been desiring to visit you⟧ (⟦i:i.e.⟧ I desire and have long desired).
Imperfect Indicative.
1. The Imperfect primarily denotes action ⟦i:going on in past time⟧; as,—
⟦b:librum legēbam⟧, ⟦i:I was reading a book⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. This force makes the Imperfect especially adapted to serve as the tense of ⟦i:description⟧ (as opposed to mere ⟦i:narration⟧).
2. From the notion of action ⟦i:going on⟧, there easily develops the notion of ⟦i:repeated⟧ or ⟦i:customary⟧ action; as,—
⟦b:lēgātōs interrogābat⟧, ⟦i:he kept asking the envoys⟧;
⟦b:C. Duīlium vidēbam puer⟧, ⟦i:as a boy I often used to see Gaius Duilius⟧.
3. The Imperfect often denotes an attempted action ('Conative Imperfect') or an action as beginning ('Inceptive Imperfect'); as,—
⟦b:hostēs nostrōs intrā mūnītiōnēs prōgredī prohibēbant⟧, ⟦i:the enemy tried to prevent⟧ (⟦b:prohibēbant⟧) ⟦i:our men from advancing within the fortifications⟧ ('Conative');
⟦b:ad proelium sē expediēbant⟧, ⟦i:they were beginning to get ready for battle⟧ ('Inceptive').
4. The Imperfect, with ⟦b:jam⟧, ⟦b:jam diū⟧, ⟦b:jam dūdum⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧, is sometimes used of an action which had been continuing some time; as,—
⟦b:domicilium Rōmae multōs jam annōs habēbat⟧, ⟦i:he had had his residence at Rome for many years⟧ (⟦i:i.e.⟧ he had it at this time and had long had it).
Future Indicative.
1. The Latin is much more exact in the use of the Future than is the English. We say: '⟦i:If he comes, I shall be glad⟧,' where we really mean: '⟦i:If he shall come⟧,' ⟦i:etc.⟧ In such cases the Latin rarely admits the Present, but generally employs the Future.
2. Sometimes the Future has Imperative force; as, ⟦b:dīcēs⟧, ⟦i:say!⟧
Perfect Indicative.
⟦i:A.⟧ PRESENT PERFECT. Several Present Perfects denote the ⟦i:state resulting from a completed act⟧, and so seem equivalent to the Present; as,—
⟦b:nōvī⟧, ⟦b:cognōvī⟧, ⟦i:I know⟧ (lit. ⟦i:I have become acquainted with⟧);
⟦b:cōnsuēvī⟧, ⟦i:I am wont⟧ (lit. ⟦i:I have become accustomed⟧).
⟦i:B.⟧ HISTORICAL PERFECT. The Historical Perfect is the tense of ⟦i:narration⟧ (as opposed to the Imperfect, the tense of ⟦i:description⟧); as,—
⟦b:Rēgulus in senātum vēnit, mandāta exposuit, reddī captivōs negāvit esse ūtile⟧, ⟦i:Regulus came into the Senate, set forth his commission, said it was useless for captives to be returned⟧.
1. Occasionally the Historical Perfect is used of a general truth ('Gnomic Perfect').
Pluperfect Indicative.
The Latin Pluperfect, like the English Past Perfect, denotes an act ⟦i:completed in the past⟧; as,—
⟦b:Caesar Rhēnum trānsīre dēcrēverat, sed nāvēs deerant⟧, ⟦i:Caesar had decided to cross the Rhine, but had no boats⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. In those verbs whose Perfect has Present force (§ 262, ⟦i:A⟧), the Pluperfect has the force of an Imperfect; as,—
⟦b:nōveram⟧, ⟦i:I knew⟧.
Future Perfect Indicative.
The Future Perfect denotes an action ⟦i:completed in future time⟧. Thus:—
⟦b:scrībam epistulam, cum redieris⟧, ⟦i:I will write the letter when you have returned⟧ (lit. ⟦i:when you shall have returned⟧).
⟦i:a⟧. The Latin is much more exact in the use of the Future Perfect than the English, which commonly employs the Present Perfect instead of the Future Perfect.
⟦i:b⟧. In those verbs whose Perfect has Present force (§ 262, ⟦i:A⟧) the Future Perfect has the force of a Future; as,—
⟦b:nōverō⟧, ⟦i:I shall know⟧.
Epistolary Tenses.
In letters the writer often uses tenses which are not appropriate at the time of writing, but which will be so at the time when his letter is received; he thus employs the Imperfect and the Perfect for the Present, and the Pluperfect for the Present Perfect; as,—
⟦b:nihil habēbam quod scrīberem, neque enim novī quidquam audieram et ad tuās omnēs epistulās jam rescrīpseram⟧, ⟦i:I have nothing to write, for I have heard no news and have already answered all your letters⟧.

title: Tenses of the Subjunctive
text:
⟦i:A.⟧ ⟦b:In Independent sentences⟧. See §§ 272-280.
⟦i:B.⟧ ⟦b:In Dependent Sentences⟧. In dependent sentences the tenses of the subjunctive usually conform to the so-called
Sequence of Tenses.
1. In the Subjunctive the Present and Perfect are Principal tenses, the Imperfect and Pluperfect, Historical.
2. By the Sequence of Tenses Principal tenses are followed by Principal, Historical by Historical. Thus:—
PRINCIPAL SEQUENCE,—
⟦b:videō quid faciās⟧, ⟦i:I see what you are doing⟧.
⟦b:vidēbō quid faciās⟧, ⟦i:I shall see what you are doing⟧.
⟦b:vīderō quid faciās⟧, ⟦i:I shall have seen what you are doing⟧.
⟦b:videō quid fēcerīs⟧, ⟦i:I see what you have done⟧.
⟦b:vidēbō quid fēcerīs⟧, ⟦i:I shall see what you have done⟧.
⟦b:vīderō quid fēcerīs⟧, ⟦i:I shall have seen what you have done⟧.
HISTORICAL SEQUENCE,—
⟦b:vidēbam quid facerēs⟧, ⟦i:I saw what you were doing⟧.
⟦b:vīdī quid facerēs⟧, ⟦i:I saw what you were doing⟧.
⟦b:vīderam quid facerēs⟧, ⟦i:I had seen what you were doing⟧.
⟦b:vidēbam quid fēcissēs⟧, ⟦i:I saw what you had done⟧.
⟦b:vīdī quid fēcissēs⟧, ⟦i:I saw what you had done⟧.
⟦b:vīderam quid fēcissēs⟧, ⟦i:I had seen what you had done⟧.
3. The Present and Imperfect Subjunctive denote incomplete action, the Perfect and Pluperfect completed action, exactly as in the Indicative.
Peculiarities of Sequence.
1. The Perfect Indicative is usually an historical tense (even when translated in English as a Present Perfect), and so is followed by the Imperfect and Pluperfect Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:dēmōnstrāvī quārē ad causam accēderem⟧, ⟦i:I have shown why I took the case⟧ (lit. ⟦i:I showed why⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧).
2. A dependent Perfect Infinitive is treated as an historical tense wherever, if resolved into an equivalent Indicative, it would be historical; as,—
⟦b:videor ostendisse quālēs deī essent⟧, ⟦i:I seem to have shown of what nature the gods are⟧ (⟦b:ostendisse⟧ here corresponds to an Indicative, ⟦b:ostendī⟧, ⟦i:I showed⟧).
3. The Historical Present is sometimes regarded as a principal tense, sometimes as historical. Thus:—
⟦b:Sulla suōs hortātur ut fortī animō sint⟧, ⟦i:Sulla exhorts his soldiers to be stout-hearted⟧;
⟦b:Gallōs hortātur ut arma caperent⟧, ⟦i:he exhorted the Gauls to take arms⟧.
4. Conditional sentences of the 'contrary-to-fact' type are not affected by the principles for the Sequence of Tenses; as,—
⟦b:honestum tāle est ut, vel sī ignōrārent id hominēs, suā tamen pulchritūdine laudabīle esset⟧, ⟦i:virtue is such a thing that even if men were ignorant of it, it would still be worthy of praise for its own loveliness⟧.
5. In conditional sentences of the 'contrary-to-fact' type the Imperfect Subjunctive is usually treated as an Historical tense; as,—
⟦b:sī sōlōs eōs dīcerēs miserōs, quibus moriendum esset, nēminem tū quidem eōrum quī vīverent exciperēs⟧, ⟦i:if you called only those wretched who must die, you would except no one of those who live⟧.
6. In clauses of Result and some others, the Perfect Subjunctive is sometimes used as an historical tense. Thus:—
⟦b:rēx tantum mōtus est, ut Tissaphernem hostem jūdicārit⟧, ⟦i:the king was so much moved that he adjudged Tissaphernes an enemy⟧.
This construction is rare in Cicero, but frequent in Nepos and subsequent historians. The Perfect Subjunctive in this use represents a result simply ⟦i:as a fact without reference to the continuance of the act⟧, and therefore corresponds to an Historical Perfect Indicative of direct statement. Thus, ⟦b:jūdicārit⟧ in the above example corresponds to ⟦b:adjūdicāvit⟧, ⟦i:he adjudged⟧. To denote a result as ⟦i:something continuous⟧, all writers use the Imperfect Subjunctive after historical tenses.
7. Sometimes perspicuity demands that the ordinary principles of Sequence be abandoned altogether. Thus:
⟦i:a⟧) We may have the Present or Perfect Subjunctive after an historical tense; as,—
⟦b:Verrēs Siciliam ita perdidit ut ea restituī nōn possit⟧, ⟦i:Verres so ruined Sicily that it cannot be restored⟧ (Direct statement: ⟦b:nōn potest restitui⟧);
⟦b:ārdēbat Hortēnsius dīcendī cupiditāte sīc, ut in nūllō flagrantius studium vīderim⟧, ⟦i:Hortensius burned so with eagerness to speak that I have seen in no one a greater desire⟧ (Direct statement: ⟦b:in nūllō vīdī⟧, ⟦i:I have seen in no one⟧).
NOTE.—This usage is different from that cited under 6. Here, by neglect of Sequence, the Perfect is used, though a principal tense; there the Perfect was used as an historical tense.
⟦i:b⟧) We may have a principal tense followed by the Perfect Subjunctive used historically; as,—
⟦b:nesciō quid causae fuerit cūr nūllās ad mē litterās darēs⟧, ⟦i:I do not know what reason there was why you did not send me a letter⟧.
Here ⟦b:fuerit⟧ is historical, as is shown by the following Imperfect Subjunctive.
Method of Expressing Future Time in the Subjunctive.
The Future and Future Perfect, which are lacking to the Latin Subjunctive, are supplied in subordinate clauses as follows:—
1.
⟦i:a⟧) The Future is supplied by the Present after principal tenses, by the Imperfect after historical tenses.
⟦i:b⟧) The Future Perfect is supplied by the Perfect after principal tenses, by the Pluperfect after historical tenses.
This is especially frequent when the context clearly shows, by the presence of a future tense in the main clause, that the reference is to future time. Thus:—
⟦b:Gallī pollicentur sē factūrōs, quae Caesar imperet⟧, ⟦i:the Gauls promise they will do what Caesar shall order⟧;
⟦b:Gallī pollicēbantur sē factūrōs, quae Caesar imperāret⟧, ⟦i:the Gauls promised they would do what Caesar should order⟧;
⟦b:Gallī pollicentur sē factūrōs quae Caesar imperāverit⟧, ⟦i:the Gauls promise they will do what Caesar shall have ordered⟧;
⟦b:Gallī pollicēbantur sē factūrōs quae Caesar imperāvisset⟧, ⟦i:the Gauls promised they would do what Caesar should have ordered.⟧
2. Even where the context does not contain a Future tense in the main clause, Future time is often expressed in the subordinate clauses by the Present and Imperfect Subjunctive. Thus:—
⟦b:timeō nē veniat⟧, ⟦i:I am afraid he will come⟧;
⟦b:Caesar exspectābat quid cōnsilī hostēs caperent⟧, ⟦i:Caesar was waiting to see what plan the enemy would adopt⟧.
3. Where greater definiteness is necessary, the periphrastic forms in ⟦b:-ūrus sim⟧ and ⟦b:-ūrus essem⟧ are employed, especially in clauses of Result, Indirect Questions, and after ⟦b:nōn dubitō quīn⟧; as,—
⟦b:nōn dubitō quīn pater ventūrus sit⟧, ⟦i:I do not doubt that my father will come⟧;
⟦b:nōn dubitābam quīn pater ventūrus esset⟧, ⟦i:I did not doubt that my father would come⟧.
4. Where the verb has no Future Active Participle, or where it stands in the passive voice, its Future character may be indicated by the use of the particles ⟦b:mox⟧, ⟦b:brevī⟧, ⟦b:statim⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧, in connection with the Present and Imperfect Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:nōn dubitō quīn tē mox hūjus reī paeniteat⟧, ⟦i:I do not doubt that you will soon repent of this thing;⟧
⟦b:nōn dubitābam quīn haec rēs brevī cōnficerētur⟧, ⟦i:I did not doubt that this thing would soon be fnished.⟧

title: Tenses of the Infinitive
text:
1. The tenses of the Infinitive denote time not absolutely, but ⟦i:with reference to the verb on which they depend.⟧ Thus:—
⟦i:a⟧) The Present Infinitive represents an act as ⟦i:contemporaneous with⟧ the time of the verb on which it depends; as,—
⟦b:vidētur honōrēs adsequī⟧, ⟦i:he seems to be gaining honors⟧;
⟦b:vidēbātur honōrēs adsequī⟧, ⟦i:he seemed to be gaining honors⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) The Perfect Infinitive represents an act as ⟦i:prior to⟧ the time of the verb on which it depends; as,—
⟦b:vidētur honōrēs adsecūtus esse⟧, ⟦i:he seems to have gained honors⟧;
⟦b:vīsus est honōrēs adsecūtus esse⟧, ⟦i:he seemed to have gained honors⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) The Future Infinitive represents an act as ⟦i:subsequent to⟧ that of the verb on which it depends; as,—
⟦b:vidētur honōrēs adsecūtūrus esse⟧, ⟦i:he seems to be about to gain honors⟧;
⟦b:vīsus est honōrēs adsecūtūrus esse⟧, ⟦i:he seemed to be about to gain honors⟧.
2. Where the English says '⟦i:ought to have done⟧,' '⟦i:might have done⟧,' ⟦i:etc.⟧, the Latin uses ⟦b:dēbuī⟧, ⟦b:oportuit⟧, ⟦b:potuī⟧ (⟦b:dēbēbam⟧, ⟦b:oportēbat⟧, ⟦b:poteram⟧), with the Present Infinitive; as,—
⟦b:dēbuit dīcere⟧, ⟦i:he ought to have said⟧ (lit. ⟦i:owed it to say⟧);
⟦b:opōrtuit venīre⟧, ⟦i:he ought to have come⟧;
⟦b:potuit vidēre⟧, ⟦i:he might have seen⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Oportuit⟧, ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:nōlō⟧ (and in poetry some other verbs), may take a Perfect Infinitive instead of the Present; as,—
⟦b:hōc jam prīdem factum esse oportuit⟧, ⟦i:this ought long ago to have been done⟧.
3. PERIPHRASTIC FUTURE INFINITIVE. Verbs that have no Participial Stem, express the Future Infinitive Active and Passive by ⟦b:fore ut⟧ or ⟦b:futūrum esse ut⟧, with the Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:spērō fore ut tē paeniteat levitātis⟧, ⟦i:I hope you will repent of your fickleness⟧ (lit. ⟦i:hope it will happen that you repent⟧);
⟦b:spērō futūrum esse ut hostēs arceantur⟧, ⟦i:I hope that the enemy will be kept off⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. The Periphrastic Future Infinitive is often used, especially in the Passive, even in case of verbs which have the Participial Stem; as,—
⟦b:spērō fore ut hostēs vincantur⟧, ⟦i:I hope the enemy will be conquered⟧.
4. Passives and Deponents sometimes form a Future Perfect Infinitive with ⟦b:fore⟧; as,—
⟦b:spērō epistulam scrīptam fore⟧, ⟦i:I hope the letter will have been written⟧;
⟦b:dīcō mē satis adeptum fore⟧, ⟦i:I say that I shall have gained enough⟧.
The Indicative in Independent Sentences.

title: Moods in Independent Sentences
Volitive Subjunctive
text: The Volitive Subjunctive represents the action ⟦i:as willed⟧. It always implies authority on the part of the speaker, and has the following varieties:—

title: Hortatory Subjunctive
Jussive Subjunctive
Prohibitive Subjunctive
text:
The Subjunctive is used in the second and third persons singular and plural, with ⟦b:nē⟧, to express ⟦i:a prohibition⟧. Both Present and Perfect occur, and without appreciable difference of meaning; as,—
⟦b:nē repugnētis⟧, ⟦i:do not resist!⟧
⟦b:tū vērō istam nē relīquerīs⟧, ⟦i:don't leave her!⟧
⟦b:impiī nē plācāre audeant deōs⟧, ⟦i:let not the impious dare to appease the gods!⟧
⟦i:a⟧. Neither of these constructions is frequent in classical prose.
⟦i:b⟧. A commoner method of expressing a prohibition in the second person is by the use of ⟦b:nōlī⟧ (⟦b:nōlīte⟧) with a following infinitive, or by ⟦b:cavē⟧ or ⟦b:cavē nē⟧ with the Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:nōlī hōc facere⟧, ⟦i:don't do this⟧ (lit. ⟦i:be unwilling to do⟧)!
⟦b:nōlīte mentīrī⟧, ⟦i:do not lie!⟧
⟦b:cavē ignōscās, cavē tē misereat⟧, ⟦i:do not forgive, do not pity!⟧
⟦b:cavē nē haec faciās⟧, ⟦i:do not do this⟧ (lit. ⟦i:take care lest you do⟧)!

title: Deliberative Subjunctive
text:
The Deliberative Subjunctive is used ⟦i:in questions and exclamations implying doubt, indignation, the impossibility of an act, obligation, or propriety⟧. The Present is used referring to present time, the Imperfect referring to past. The negative is ⟦b:nōn⟧. Thus:—
⟦b:quid faciam⟧, ⟦i:what shall I do?⟧
⟦b:ego redeam⟧, ⟦i:I go back!⟧
⟦b:huic cēdāmus! hūjus condiciōnēs audiāmus!⟧ ⟦i:are we to bow to him! are we to listen to his terms!⟧
⟦b:quid facerem⟧, ⟦i:what was I to do?⟧
⟦b:hunc ego nōn dīligam⟧, ⟦i:should I not cherish this man?⟧
⟦i:a⟧. These Deliberative Questions are usually purely Rhetorical in character, and do not expect an answer.

title: Concessive Subjunctive
Optative Subjunctive
text:
The Optative Subjunctive occurs in expressions of ⟦i:wishing⟧. The negative is regularly ⟦b:nē⟧.
1. The Present Tense, often accompanied by ⟦b:utinam⟧, is used where the wish is conceived of ⟦i:as possible⟧.
⟦b:dī istaec prohibeant⟧, ⟦i:may the gods prevent that!⟧
⟦b:falsus utinam vātēs sim⟧, ⟦i:oh that I may be a false prophet!⟧
⟦b:nē veniant⟧, ⟦i:may they not come!⟧
2. The Imperfect expresses, in the form of a wish, the ⟦i:regret that something is not so now⟧; the Pluperfect that something ⟦i:was not so in the past⟧. The Imperfect and Pluperfect are regularly accompanied by ⟦b:utinam⟧; as,—
⟦b:utinam istud ex animō dīcerēs⟧, ⟦i:would that you were saying that in earnest⟧ (⟦i:i.e.⟧ I regret that you are not saying it in earnest);
⟦b:Pēlīdēs utinam vītāsset Apollinis arcūs⟧, ⟦i:would that Achilles had escaped the bow of Apollo⟧;
⟦b:utinam nē nātus essem⟧, ⟦i:would that I had not been born⟧.

title: Potential Subjunctive
Moods in Dependent Clauses
text:
1. Clauses of Purpose are introduced most commonly by ⟦b:ut (utī), quō⟧ (⟦i:that⟧, ⟦i:in order that⟧), ⟦b:nē⟧ (⟦i:in order that not, lest⟧), and stand in the Subjunctive, as,—
⟦b:edimus ut vīvāmus⟧, ⟦i:we eat that we may live;⟧
⟦b:adjūtā mē quō hōc fīat facilius⟧, ⟦i:help me, in order that this may be done more easily;⟧
⟦b:portās clausit, nē quam oppidānī injūriam acciperent⟧, ⟦i:he closed the gates, lest the townspeople should receive any injury.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Quō⟧, as a rule, is employed only when the purpose clause contains a comparative or a comparative idea. Occasional exceptions occur; as,—
⟦b:haec faciunt quō Chremētem absterreant⟧, ⟦i:they are doing this in order to frighten Chremes.⟧
⟦i:b⟧. ⟦b:Ut nē⟧ is sometimes found instead of ⟦b:nē⟧. Thus:—
⟦b:ut nē quid neglegenter agāmus⟧, ⟦i:in order that we may not do anything carelessly⟧.
⟦i:c⟧. ⟦b:Ut nōn⟧ (not ⟦b:nē⟧) is used where the negation belongs to some single word, instead of to the purpose clause as a whole. Thus:—
⟦b:ut nōn ējectus ad aliēnōs, sed invītātus ad tuōs videāre⟧, ⟦i:that you may seem not driven out among strangers, but invited to your own friends.⟧
⟦i:d⟧. To say '⟦i:and that not⟧' or '⟦i:or that not⟧,' the Latin regularly uses ⟦b:nēve (neu)⟧; as,—
⟦b:ut eārum rērum vīs minuerētur, neu pontī nocērent⟧, ⟦i:that the violence of these things might be lessened, and that they might not harm the bridge⟧;
⟦b:profūgit, nē caperētur nēve interficerētur⟧, ⟦i:he fled, that he might not be captured or killed.⟧
⟦i:e⟧. But ⟦b:neque⟧ (for ⟦b:nēve⟧) is sometimes used in a second Purpose Clause when ⟦b:ut⟧ stands in the first, and, after the Augustan era, even when the first clause is introduced by ⟦b:nē⟧.
⟦i:f⟧. Purpose Clauses sometimes stand in apposition with a preceding noun or pronoun: as,—
⟦b:hāc causā, ut pācem habērent⟧, ⟦i:on this account, that they might have peace.⟧
2. A Relative Pronoun (⟦b:quī⟧) or Adverb (⟦b:ubi⟧, ⟦b:unde⟧, ⟦b:quō⟧) is frequently used to introduce a Purpose Clause; as,—
⟦b:Helvētiī lēgātōs mittunt, quī dīcerent⟧, ⟦i:the Helvetii sent envoys to say⟧ (lit. ⟦i:who should say⟧);
⟦b:haec habuī, dē senectūte quae dīcerem⟧, ⟦i:I had these things to say about old age⟧;
⟦b:nōn habēbant quō sē reciperent⟧, ⟦i:they had no place to which to flee⟧ (lit. ⟦i:whither they might flee⟧).
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Quī⟧ in such clauses is equivalent to ⟦b:ut is⟧, ⟦b:ut ego⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; ⟦b:ubi⟧ to ⟦b:ut ibi⟧; ⟦b:unde⟧ to ⟦b:ut inde⟧; ⟦b:quō⟧ to ⟦b:ut eō⟧.
3. Relative Clauses of purpose follow ⟦b:dignus⟧, ⟦b:indignus⟧, and ⟦b:idōneus⟧; as,—
⟦b:idōneus fuit nēmō quem imitārēre⟧, ⟦i:there was no one suitable for you to imitate⟧ (⟦i:cf⟧. ⟦b:nēmō fuit quem imitārēre⟧, ⟦i:there was no one for you to imitate⟧);
⟦b:dignus est quī aliquandō imperet⟧, ⟦i:he is worthy to rule sometime⟧.
4. Purpose Clauses often depend upon something to be supplied from the context instead of upon the principal verb of their own sentences; as,—
⟦b:ut haec omnia omittam, abiimus⟧, ⟦i:to pass over all this,⟧ (⟦i:I will say that⟧) ⟦i:we departed⟧.
Clauses of Characteristic.
1. A relative clause used ⟦i:to express a quality or characteristic of a general or indefinite antecedent⟧ is called a Clause of Characteristic, and usually stands in the Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:multa sunt, quae mentem acuant⟧, ⟦i:there are many things which sharpen the wits.⟧
Clauses of Characteristic are opposed to those relative clauses which are used merely to state some fact about a definite antecedent, and which therefore take the Indicative; as,—
⟦b:Catō, senex jūcundus, quī Sapiēns appellātus est⟧, ⟦i:Cato, a delightful old man, who was called 'The Wise.'⟧
The Clause of Characteristic implies '⟦i:a person of the sort that does something⟧'; the Indicative relative clause implies '⟦i:a particular person who does something⟧.'
2. Clauses of Characteristic are used especially after such expressions as, ⟦b:est quī⟧; ⟦b:sunt quī⟧; ⟦b:nēmō est quī⟧; ⟦b:nūllus est quī⟧; ⟦b:ūnus est quī⟧; ⟦b:sōlus est quī⟧; ⟦b:quis est quī⟧; ⟦b:is quī⟧; ⟦i:etc.⟧ Thus:—
⟦b:sunt quī dīcant⟧, ⟦i:there are (some) who say⟧;
⟦b:nēmō est quī nesciat⟧, ⟦i:there is nobody who is ignorant⟧;
⟦b:sapientia est ūna quae maestitiam pellat⟧, ⟦i:philosophy is the only thing that drives away sorrow⟧;
⟦b:quae cīvitās est quae nōn ēvertī possit⟧, ⟦i:what state is there that cannot be overthrown?⟧
⟦b:nōn is sum quī improbōs laudem⟧, ⟦i:I am not the sort of man that praises the wicked.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. Sometimes (very rarely in Cicero and Caesar) the clause of characteristic is used after comparatives; as,—
⟦b:nōn longius hostēs aberant quam quō tēlum adigī posset⟧, ⟦i:the enemy were not too far off for a dart to reach them⟧ (lit. ⟦i:further off than [a point] to which a dart could be cast⟧).
3. The Clause of Characteristic often conveys an accessory notion of cause (⟦i:since⟧) or opposition (⟦i:although⟧). Thus:—
⟦i:a⟧) Cause. The relative is then frequently accompanied by ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:quīppe⟧, ⟦b:utpote⟧; as,—
⟦b:ō fortūnāte adulēscēns, quī tuae virtūtis Homērum praecōnem invēnerīs⟧, ⟦i:O fortunate man, since you have found a Homer as the herald of your valor⟧;
⟦b:ut quī optimō jūre eam prōvinciam obtinuerit⟧, ⟦i:since he held that province by excellent right⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) Opposition:—
⟦b:egomet quī sērō Graecās litterās attigissem, tamen complūrēs diēs Athēnīs commorātus sum⟧, ⟦i:I, although I had taken up Greek literature late in life, nevertheless tarried several days at Athens⟧.
4. Clauses of Characteristic may also be introduced by ⟦b:quīn = quī (quae, quod) nōn⟧; as,—
⟦b:nēmō est quīn saepe audierit⟧, ⟦i:there is no one who has not often heard⟧;
⟦b:nēmō fuit mīlitum quīn vulnerārētur⟧, ⟦i:there was no one of the soldiers who was not wounded⟧.
5. Related to Clauses of Characteristic are also phrases of the type:
⟦b:quod sciam⟧, ⟦i:so far as I know⟧; ⟦b:quem⟧ (⟦b:quam⟧, ⟦b:quod⟧), ⟦b:audierim⟧, ⟦i:so far as I have heard⟧.
Clauses of Result.
1. Clauses of Result are usually introduced by ⟦b:ut⟧ (⟦i:that⟧, ⟦i:so that⟧), negative ⟦b:ut nōn⟧ (⟦i:so that not⟧), and take the Subjunctive. The main clause often contains ⟦b:tantus⟧, ⟦b:tālis⟧, ⟦b:tot⟧, ⟦b:is⟧ (= ⟦b:tālis⟧), ⟦b:tam⟧, ⟦b:ita⟧, ⟦b:sīc⟧, ⟦b:adeō⟧, or some similar word. Thus:—
⟦b:quis tam dēmēns est ut suā voluntāte maereat⟧, ⟦i:who is so senseless as to mourn of his own volition?⟧
⟦b:Siciliam ita vāstāvit ut restituī in antīquum statum nōn possit⟧, ⟦i:he so ravaged Sicily that it cannot be restored to its former condition⟧;
⟦b:mōns altissimus impendēbat, ut facile perpaucī prohibēre possent⟧, ⟦i:a very high mountain overhung, so that a very few could easily stop them⟧;
⟦b:nōn is es ut tē pudor umquam ā turpitūdine āvocārit⟧, ⟦i:you are not so constituted that shame ever called you back from baseness⟧.
2. A Result Clause is often introduced by a Relative Pronoun or Adverb, ⟦b:quī⟧ (⟦b:= ut is⟧), ⟦b:quō⟧ (⟦b:= ut eō⟧), ⟦i:etc.⟧; as,—
⟦b:nēmō est tam senex quī sē annum nōn putet posse vīvere⟧, ⟦i:nobody is so old as not to think he can live a year⟧;
⟦b:habētis eum cōnsulem quī pārēre vestrīs dēcrētīs nōn dubitet⟧, ⟦i:you have a consul such as does not hesitate to obey your decrees⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. These Relative Clauses of Result are closely related to the Clause of Characteristic, and sometimes it is difficult to distinguish the two constructions. It is best to class the relative clause as one of Characteristic, unless the result idea is clear and unmistakable.
3. Result clauses may also be introduced by ⟦b:quīn = ut nōn⟧; as,—
⟦b:nihil tam difficile est quīn quaerendō invēstīgārī possit⟧, ⟦i:nothing is so difficult that it cannot be discovered by searching⟧;
⟦b:nēmō est tam fortis quīn reī novitāte perturbētur⟧, ⟦i:no one is so steadfast as not to be thrown into confusion by a strange occurrence⟧.
4. Note the use of ⟦b:quam ut⟧ (sometimes ⟦b:quam⟧ alone) to denote Result after comparatives; as,—
⟦b:urbs erat mūnītior quam ut prīmō impetū capī posset⟧, ⟦i:the city was too strongly fortified to be taken at the first attack⟧ (lit. ⟦i:more strongly fortified than [so] that it could be taken, etc.⟧).
Causal Clauses.
Causal clauses are introduced chiefly by the following particles:—
1. ⟦b:Quod⟧, ⟦b:quia⟧, ⟦b:quoniam⟧.
2. ⟦b:Cum⟧.
3. ⟦b:Quandō⟧.
The use of moods is as follows:—
1. ⟦b:Quod⟧, ⟦b:quia⟧, ⟦b:quoniam⟧ take the Indicative when the reason is ⟦i:that of the writer or speaker;⟧ they take the Subjunctive when the reason is viewed ⟦i:as that of another.⟧ Thus:—
⟦b:Parthōs timeō quod diffīdō cōpiīs nostrīs⟧, ⟦i:I fear the Parthians, because I distrust our troops⟧.
⟦b:Themistoclēs, quia nōn tūtus erat, Corcyram dēmigrāvit⟧, ⟦i:Themistocles, since he was not safe, moved to Corcyra⟧.
⟦b:neque mē vīxisse paenitet, quoniam bene vīxī⟧, ⟦i:I do not regret having lived, since I have lived well⟧.
⟦b:Sōcratēs accūsātus est quod corrumperet juventūtem⟧, ⟦i:Socrates was arraigned on the ground that he was corrupting the young⟧. (Here the reason is not that of the writer but of the accuser. Hence the Subjunctive.)
⟦b:Haeduī Caesarī grātiās ēgērunt quod sē perīculō līberāvisset⟧, ⟦i:the Haedui thanked Caesar because he had delivered them from danger⟧. (The reason of the Haedui.)
⟦b:quoniam Miltiadēs dīcere nōn posset, verba prō eō fēcit Tīsagorās⟧, ⟦i:since Miltiades could not speak, Tisagoras spoke for him⟧. (The reason of Tisagoras.)
⟦b:noctū ambulābat Themistoclēs, quod somnum capere nōn posset⟧, ⟦i:Themistocles used to walk at night because (as he said) he couldn't sleep⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Verbs of ⟦i:thinking⟧ and ⟦i:saying⟧ often stand in the Subjunctive in causal clauses as though the act of thinking or saying, and not the contents of the thought or language, constituted the reason. Thus:—
⟦b:Bellovacī suum numerum nōn complēvērunt quod sē suō nōmine cum Rōmānīs bellum gestūrōs dīcerent⟧, ⟦i:the Bellovaci did not furnish their complement, because they said they were going to wage war with the Romans on their own account⟧.
⟦i:b⟧. ⟦b:Nōn quod⟧, ⟦b:nōn quō⟧ (by attraction for ⟦b:nōn eō quod⟧), ⟦b:nōn quia⟧, ⟦i:not that⟧, ⟦i:not because⟧; and ⟦b:nōn quod nōn⟧, ⟦b:nōn quō nōn⟧, ⟦b:nōn quīn⟧, ⟦i:not that ... not⟧; ⟦i:not because ... not⟧; ⟦i:not but that⟧, are usually employed merely to introduce a hypothetical reason, and hence take the Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:id fēcī, nōn quod vōs hanc dēfēnsiōnem dēsīderāre arbitrārer, sed ut omnēs intellegerent⟧, ⟦i:this I did, not because I thought you needed this defense, but that all might perceive⟧;
⟦b:Crassō commendātiōnem nōn sum pollicitus, nōn quīn eam valitūram apud tē arbitrārer, sed egēre mihi commendātiōne nōn vidēbātur⟧, ⟦i:I did not promise a recommendation to Crassus, not that I did not think it would have weight with you, but because he did not seem to me to need recommendation⟧.
⟦i:c⟧. But clauses introduced by ⟦b:nōn quod⟧, ⟦b:nōn quīa⟧ take the Indicative ⟦i:if they state a fact⟧, even though that fact is denied to be the reason for something; as,—
⟦b:hōc ita sentiō, nōn quia sum ipse augur, sed quia sīc exīstimāre nōs est necesse⟧, ⟦i:this I think, not because I am myself an augur (which I really am), but because it is necessary for us to think so⟧.
2. ⟦b:Cum⟧ causal regularly takes the Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:quae cum īta sint⟧, ⟦i:since this is so⟧;
⟦b:cum sīs mortālis, quae mortālia sunt, cūrā⟧, ⟦i:since you are mortal, care for what is mortal⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Note the phrase ⟦b:cum praesertim (praesertim cum)⟧, ⟦i:especially since;⟧ as,—
⟦b:Haeduōs accūsat, praesertim cum eōrum precibus adductus bellum suscēperit⟧, ⟦i:he blamed the Haedui, especially since he had undertaken the war at their entreaties⟧.
3. ⟦b:Quandō⟧ (less frequent than the other causal particles) governs the Indicative; as,—
⟦b:id omittō, quandō vōbīs ita placet⟧, ⟦i:I pass over that, since you so wish⟧.
Temporal Clauses introduced by ⟦i:Postquam⟧, ⟦i:Ut⟧, ⟦i:Ubi⟧, ⟦i:Simul ac⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧
1. ⟦b:Postquam⟧ (⟦b:posteāquam⟧), ⟦i:after⟧; ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:ubi⟧, ⟦i:when⟧; ⟦b:cum prīmum⟧, ⟦b:simul⟧, ⟦b:simul ac⟧ (⟦b:simul atque⟧), ⟦i:as soon as⟧, when used to refer ⟦i:to a single past act⟧ regularly take the Perfect Indicative; as,—
⟦b:Epamīnōndās postquam audīvit vīcisse Boeōtiōs, 'Satis' inquit 'vīxī,'⟧ ⟦i:Epaminondas, after he heard that the Boeotians had conquered, said, 'I have lived enough;'⟧
⟦b:id ut audīvit, Corcyram dēmigrāvit⟧, ⟦i:when he heard this, he moved to Corcyra⟧;
⟦b:Caesar cum prīmum potuit, ad exercitum contendit⟧, ⟦i:Caesar, as soon as he could, hurried to the army⟧;
⟦b:ubi dē Caesaris adventū certiōrēs factī sunt, lēgātōs ad eum mittunt⟧, ⟦i:when they were informed of Caesar's arrival, they sent envoys to him⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. The Historical Present may take the place of the Perfect in this construction.
2. To denote ⟦i:the repeated occurrence⟧ of an act, ⟦b:ut, ubi, simul atque⟧, ⟦i:as often as⟧, when following an historical tense, take the Pluperfect Indicative (compare §§ 288, 3; 302, 3); as,—
⟦b:ut quisque Verris animum offenderat, in lautumiās statim coniciēbātur⟧, ⟦i:whenever anybody had offended Verres's feelings, he was forthwith put in the stone-quarry⟧;
⟦b:hostēs, ubi aliquōs ēgredientēs cōnspexerant, adoriēbantur⟧, ⟦i:whenever the enemy had seen any men disembarking, they attacked them⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. In Livy and succeeding historians the Imperfect and Pluperfect Subjunctive are used to denote this repeated occurrence of an act ('Indefinite Frequency'); as,—
⟦b:id ubi dīxisset hastam mittēbat⟧, ⟦i:whenever he had said that, he hurled a spear⟧.
3. Occasionally the above conjunctions are followed by the Pluperfect Indicative of a single occurrence. This is regularly the case with ⟦b:postquam⟧ in expressions denoting a definite interval of time (days, months, years, ⟦i:etc.⟧), such as ⟦b:post tertium annum quam⟧, ⟦b:trienniō postquam⟧. Thus:—
⟦b:quīnque post diēbus quam Lūcā discesserat, ad Sardiniam vēnit⟧ ⟦i:five days after he had departed from Luca he came to Sardinia⟧;
⟦b:postquam occupātae Syrācūsae erant, profectus est Carthāginem⟧, ⟦i:after Syracuse had been seized, he set out for Carthage⟧.
4. The Imperfect Indicative also sometimes occurs, to denote ⟦i:a continued state;⟧ as,—
⟦b:postquam Rōmam adventābant, senātus cōnsultus est⟧, ⟦i:after they were on the march toward Rome, the Senate was consulted⟧;
⟦b:postquam strūctī utrimque stābant⟧, ⟦i:after they had been drawn up on both sides and were in position⟧.
5. ⟦b:Rarely postquam⟧, ⟦b:posteāquam⟧, following the analogy of ⟦b:cum⟧, take the Subjunctive, but only in the historical tenses; as,—
⟦b:posteāquam sūmptuōsa fieri fūnera coepissent, lēge sublāta sunt⟧, ⟦i:after funerals had begun to be elaborate, they were done away with by law⟧.
Temporal Clauses introduced by ⟦i:Cum⟧.
⟦i:A.⟧ ⟦b:Cum⟧ REFERRING TO THE PAST.
1. ⟦b:Cum⟧, when referring to the past, takes,—
⟦i:A.⟧ The Indicative (Imperfect, Historical Perfect, or Pluperfect) to denote ⟦i:the point of time at which⟧ something occurs.
⟦i:B.⟧ The Subjunctive (Imperfect or Pluperfect) to denote ⟦i:the situation or circumstances under which⟧ something occurs.
Examples:—
INDICATIVE.
⟦b:an tum erās cōnsul, cum in Palātiō mea domus ārdēbat⟧, ⟦i:or were you consul at the time when my house burned up on the Palatine?⟧
⟦b:crēdō tum cum Sicilia flōrēbat opibus et cōpiīs magna artificia fuisse in eā īnsulā⟧, ⟦i:I believe that at the time when Sicily was powerful in riches and resources there were great crafts in that island⟧;
⟦b:eō tempore pāruit cum pārēre necesse erat⟧, ⟦i:he obeyed at the time when it was necessary to obey⟧;
⟦b:illō diē, cum est lāta lēx dē mē⟧, ⟦i:on that day when the law concerning me was passed⟧.
SUBJUNCTIVE.
⟦b:Lysander cum vellet Lycūrgī lēgēs commūtāre, prohibitus est⟧, ⟦i:when Lysander desired to change the laws of Lycurgus, he was prevented⟧;
⟦b:Pythagorās cum in geōmetriā quiddam novī invēnisset, Mūsīs bovem immolāsse dīcitur⟧, ⟦i:when Pythagoras had discovered something new in geometry, he is said to have sacrificed an ox to the Muses⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Note that the Indicative is much less frequent in such clauses than the Subjunctive, and is regularly confined to those cases where the main clause has ⟦b:tum⟧, ⟦b:eō diē⟧, ⟦b:eō annō⟧, ⟦b:eō tempore⟧ or some similar correlative of the ⟦b:cum⟧. Sometimes it depends entirely upon the point of view of the writer whether he shall employ the Indicative or Subjunctive.
2. ⟦b:Cum Inversum⟧. When the logical order of the clauses is inverted, we find ⟦b:cum⟧ with the Perfect Indicative or Historical Present, in the sense of ⟦i:when⟧, ⟦i:when suddenly⟧. The main clause in such cases often has ⟦b:jam⟧, ⟦b:vix⟧, ⟦b:aegrē⟧, ⟦b:nōndum⟧; as,—
⟦b:jam Gallī ex oppidō fugere apparābant, cum mātrēs familiae repente prōcurrērunt⟧, ⟦i:the Gauls were already preparing to flee, when suddenly the matrons rushed forth⟧ (logically, ⟦i:the matrons rushed forth as the Gauls were preparing to flee⟧);
⟦b:Trēvirī Labiēnum adorīrī parābant, cum duās legiōnēs vēnisse cognōscunt⟧, ⟦i:the Treviri were preparing to attack, when (suddenly) they learned that two legions had arrived⟧.
3. To denote a ⟦i:recurring action⟧ in the past, ⟦b:cum⟧ is followed by the Indicative, particularly of the Pluperfect (compare §§ 287, 2; 302, 3); as,—
⟦b:cum ād aliquod oppidum vēnerat, eādem lectīcā ad cubiculum dēferēbātur⟧, ⟦i:whenever he had arrived at some town, he was (always) carried in the same litter to his room⟧;
⟦b:cum equitātus noster sē in agrōs ējēcerat, essedāriōs ex silvīs ēmittēbat⟧, ⟦i:whenever our cavalry had advanced into the fields, he would send his charioteers out from the woods⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Sometimes the Imperfect or Pluperfect Subjunctive is thus used; as,—
⟦b:saepe cum aliquem vidēret minus bene vestītum, suum amiculum dedit⟧, ⟦i:often, wherever he saw some one more poorly clothed, he gave him his own mantle⟧;
⟦b:cum prōcucurrissent, Numidae effugiēbant⟧, ⟦i:as often as they had advanced, the Numidians ran away⟧.
This construction is frequent in Livy and subsequent historians.
⟦i:B.⟧ ⟦b:Cum⟧ REFERRING TO THE PRESENT OR FUTURE.
When ⟦b:cum⟧ refers to the Present or Future it regularly takes the Indicative; as,—
⟦b:tum tua rēs agitur, pariēs cum proximus ārdet⟧, ⟦i:your own interests are at stake when your neighbor's house is burning⟧;
⟦b:cum vidēbis, tum sciēs⟧, ⟦i:when you see, then you will know.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. The Indicative of the Present or Future may denote also a ⟦i:recurring action;⟧ as,—
⟦b:stabilitās amīcitiae cōnfirmārī potest, cum hominēs cupīdinibus imperābunt⟧, ⟦i:firm friendship can be established whenever men shall control their desires.⟧
⟦i:C.⟧ OTHER USES OF ⟦b:Cum⟧.
1. ⟦b:Cum Explicative⟧. ⟦b:Cum⟧, with the Indicative, is sometimes used to indicate the identity of one act with another; as,—
⟦b:cum tacent clāmant⟧, ⟦i:their silence is a shout⟧ (lit. ⟦i:when they are silent, they shout⟧).
2. ⟦b:Cum ... tum.⟧ When ⟦b:cum ... tum⟧ mean ⟦i:both ... and⟧, the ⟦b:cum⟧-clause is in the Indicative; but when ⟦b:cum⟧ has the force of ⟦i:while⟧, ⟦i:though⟧, it may take the Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:cum tē semper dīlēxerim, tum tuīs factīs incēnsus sum⟧, ⟦i:while I have always loved you, at the same time I am stirred by your conduct⟧.
Clauses introduced by ⟦i:Antequam⟧ and ⟦i:Priusquam⟧.

title: Antequam and priusquam with the indicative
text:
⟦b:Antequam⟧ and ⟦b:priusquam⟧ (often written ⟦b:ante ... quam⟧, ⟦b:prius ... quam⟧) take the Indicative to denote ⟦i:an actual fact⟧.
1. Sometimes the Present or Future Perfect; as,—
⟦b:prius respondēs quam rogō⟧, ⟦i:you answer before I ask⟧;
⟦b:nihil contrā disputābō priusquam dīxerit⟧, ⟦i:I will say nothing in opposition, before he speaks⟧.
2. Sometimes the Perfect, especially after negative clauses; as,—
⟦b:nōn prius jugulandī fīnis fuit, quam Sulla omnēs suōs dīvitiīs explēvit⟧, ⟦i:there was no end of murder until Sulla satisfied all his henchmen with wealth⟧.

title: Temporal clauses with the subjunctive
text:
⟦b:Antequam⟧ and ⟦b:priusquam⟧ take the Subjunctive to denote an act as ⟦i:anticipated⟧.
1. Thus the Subjunctive may denote—
⟦i:a⟧) An act in preparation for which the main act takes place; as,—
⟦b:priusquam dīmicārent, foedus īctum est⟧, ⟦i:i.e. in anticipation of the fight, a treaty was struck.⟧
By an extension of this usage, the Subjunctive is sometimes used of ⟦i:general truths⟧, where the anticipatory notion has faded out; as,—
⟦b:tempestās minātur antequam surgat⟧, ⟦i:the tempest threatens before it rises⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) An act anticipated and forestalled; as,—
⟦b:priusquam tēlum adicī posset, omnis aciēs terga vertit⟧, ⟦i:before a spear could be hurled, the whole army fled.⟧
⟦i:c⟧) An act anticipated and deprecated; as,—
⟦b:animum omittunt priusquam locō dēmigrent⟧, ⟦i:they die rather than quit their post.⟧
2. After historical tenses the Imperfect Subjunctive is used, especially by some writers, where the notion of anticipation has practically vanished; as,—
⟦b:sōl antequam sē abderet fugientem vīdit Antōnium⟧, ⟦i:the sun before it set saw Antony fleeing.⟧
Clauses introduced by ⟦i:Dum⟧, ⟦i:Dōnec⟧, ⟦i:Quoad⟧.
1. ⟦b:Dum⟧, ⟦i:while⟧, regularly takes the Indicative of the Historical Present; as,—
⟦b:Alexander, dum inter prīmōrēs pugnat, sagittā ictus est⟧, ⟦i:Alexander, while he was fighting in the van, was struck by an arrow⟧;
⟦b:dum haec geruntur, in fīnēs Venellōrum pervēnit⟧, ⟦i:while these things were being done, he arrived in the territory of the Venelli⟧.
II. ⟦b:Dum⟧, ⟦b:dōnec⟧, and ⟦b:quoad⟧, ⟦i:as long as⟧, take the Indicative; as,—
⟦b:dum anima est, spēs est⟧, ⟦i:as long as there is life, there is hope⟧;
⟦b:Lacedaemoniōrum gēns fortis fuit, dum Lycūrgī lēgēs vigēbant⟧, ⟦i:the race of the Lacedaemonians was powerful, as long as the laws of Lycurgus were in force⟧;
⟦b:Catō, quoad vīxit, virtūtum laude crēvit⟧, ⟦i:Cato, at long as he lived, increased in the fame of his virtues⟧.
III. ⟦b:Dum⟧, ⟦b:dōnec⟧, and ⟦b:quoad⟧, ⟦i:until⟧, take:—
1. The Indicative, to denote ⟦i:an actual event⟧; as,—
⟦b:dōnec rediit, fuit silentium⟧, ⟦i:there was silence till he came⟧;
⟦b:ferrum in corpore retinuit, quoad renūntiātum est Boeōtiōs vīcisse⟧, ⟦i:he kept the iron in his body until word was brought that the Boeotians had conquered⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. In Livy and subsequent historians ⟦b:dum⟧ and ⟦b:dōnec⟧ in this sense often take the Subjunctive instead of the Indicative; as,—
⟦b:trepidātiōnis aliquantum ēdēbant dōnec timor quiētem fēcisset⟧, ⟦i:they showed some trepidation, until fear produced quiet⟧.
2. The Subjunctive, to denote ⟦i:anticipation⟧ or ⟦i:expectancy⟧; as,—
⟦b:exspectāvit Caesar dum nāvēs convenīrent⟧, ⟦i:Caesar waited for the ships to assemble⟧;
⟦b:dum litterae veniant, morābor⟧, ⟦i:I shall wait for the letter to come⟧.
Substantive Clauses.
A Substantive Clause is one which as a whole serves as the Subject or Object of a verb, or stands in some other case relation.
⟦i:A.⟧ Substantive Clauses developed from the Volitive.
Substantive Clauses Developed from the Volitive are used with the following classes of verbs:—
1. With verbs signifying ⟦i:to admonish⟧, ⟦i:request⟧, ⟦i:command⟧, ⟦i:urge⟧, ⟦i:persuade⟧, ⟦i:induce⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧ (conjunctions ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:nē⟧, or ⟦b:ut nē⟧); as,—
⟦b:postulō ut fīat⟧, ⟦i:I demand that it be done⟧ (dependent form of the Jussive ⟦b:fīat⟧, ⟦i:let it be done!⟧);
⟦b:ōrat, nē abeās⟧, ⟦i:he begs that you will not go away⟧;
⟦b:mīlitēs cohortātus est ut hostium impetum sustinērent⟧, ⟦i:he exhorted his soldiers to withstand the attack of the enemy⟧;
⟦b:Helvētiīs persuāsit ut exīrent⟧, ⟦i:he persuaded the Helvetii to march forth⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Jubeō⟧, ⟦i:command⟧, ⟦i:order⟧, regularly takes the Infinitive.
2. With verbs signifying ⟦i:to grant⟧, ⟦i:concede⟧, ⟦i:permit⟧, ⟦i:allow⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧ (conjunction ⟦b:ut⟧); as,—
⟦b:huic concēdō ut ea praetereat⟧, ⟦i:I allow him to pass that by⟧ (dependent form of the Jussive ⟦b:ea praetereat⟧, ⟦i:let him pass that by!⟧);
⟦b:cōnsulī permissum est ut duās legiōnēs scrīberet⟧, ⟦i:the consul was permitted to enroll two legions⟧.
3. With verbs of ⟦i:hindering⟧, ⟦i:preventing⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧ (conjunctions ⟦b:nē⟧, ⟦b:quōminus⟧, ⟦b:quīn⟧); as,—
⟦b:nē lūstrum perficeret, mors prohibuit⟧, ⟦i:death prevented him from finishing the lustrum⟧ (dependent form after past tense of ⟦b:nē lūstrum perficiat⟧, ⟦i:let him not finish⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧);
⟦b:prohibuit quōminus in ūnum coīrent⟧, ⟦i:he prevented them from coming together⟧;
⟦b:nec quīn ērumperet, prohibērī poterat⟧, ⟦i:nor could he be prevented from rushing forth⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Quīn⟧ is used only when the verb of ⟦i:hindering⟧ is accompanied by a negative, or stands in a question implying a negative; it is not ⟦i:necessarily⟧ used even then.
4. With verbs of ⟦i:deciding⟧, ⟦i:resolving⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧ (conjunctions ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:nē⟧, or ⟦b:ut nē⟧); as,—
⟦b:cōnstitueram ut prīdiē Īdūs Aquīnī manērem⟧, ⟦i:I had decided to remain at Aquinum on the 12th⟧;
⟦b:dēcrēvit senātus ut Opīmius vidēret⟧, ⟦i:the Senate decreed that Opimius should see to it⟧;
⟦b:convēnit ut ūnīs castrīs miscērentur⟧, ⟦i:it was agreed that they should be united in one camp⟧.
5. With verbs of ⟦i:striving⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧ (conjunctions ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:nē⟧, or ⟦b:ut nē⟧); as,—
⟦b:fac ut eum exōrēs⟧, ⟦i:see to it that you prevail upon him!⟧
⟦b:cūrā ut vir sīs⟧, ⟦i:see to it that you are a man!⟧
⟦b:labōrābat ut reliquās cīvitātēs adjungeret⟧, ⟦i:he was striving to join the remaining states to him⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Cōnor⟧, ⟦i:try⟧, always takes the Infinitive.
NOTE.—Verbs of all the above classes also admit the Infinitive, especially in poetry.
6. With a few other expressions, such as ⟦b:necesse est⟧, ⟦b:reliquus est⟧, ⟦b:sequitur⟧, ⟦b:licet⟧, ⟦b:oportet⟧; as,—
⟦b:sequitur ut doceam⟧, ⟦i:it remains for me to show⟧;
⟦b:licet redeās⟧, ⟦i:you may return⟧;
⟦b:oportet loquāmur⟧, ⟦i:we must speak⟧.
On the absence of ⟦b:ut⟧ with ⟦b:licet⟧ and ⟦b:oportet⟧, see paragraph 8.
7. Here also belong phrases of the type: ⟦b:nūlla causa est cūr⟧, ⟦b:quīn⟧; ⟦b:nōn est cūr⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; ⟦b:nihil est cūr⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; as,—
⟦b:nūlla causa est cūr timeam⟧, ⟦i:there is no reason why I should fear⟧ (originally Deliberative: ⟦i:why should I fear? There's no reason⟧);
⟦b:nihil est quīn dīcam⟧, ⟦i:there is no reason why I should not say⟧.
8. Many of the above classes of verbs at times take the simple Subjunctive without ⟦b:ut⟧. In such cases we must not recognize any omission of ⟦b:ut⟧, but simply an earlier form of expression which existed before the ⟦b:ut⟧-clause arose. This is regularly the case with ⟦b:necesse est⟧, ⟦b:licet⟧, and ⟦b:oportet⟧; see 6. Other examples are:—
⟦b:eōs moneō dēsinant⟧, ⟦i:I warn them to stop⟧;
⟦b:huic imperat adeat cīvitātēs⟧, ⟦i:he orders him to visit the states⟧.
⟦i:B.⟧ Substantive Clauses developed from the Optative.
Substantive Clauses Developed from the Optative occur:—
1. With verbs of ⟦i:wishing⟧, ⟦i:desiring⟧, especially ⟦b:cupiō⟧, ⟦b:optō⟧, ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:mālō⟧ (conjunctions ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:nē⟧, ⟦b:ut nē⟧); as,—
⟦b:optō ut in hōc jūdiciō nēmō improbus reperiātur⟧, ⟦i:I hope that in this court no bad man may be found⟧ (here ⟦b:ut reperiātur⟧ represents a simple optative of direct statement, ⟦i:viz.⟧ ⟦b:reperiātur⟧, ⟦i:may no bad man be found⟧!);
⟦b:cupiō nē veniat⟧, ⟦i:I desire that he may not come⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. The simple Subjunctive (without ⟦b:ut⟧) sometimes occurs with verbs of this class. (See § 295, 8.) Examples are: ⟦b:velim scrībās⟧, ⟦i:I wish you would write⟧; ⟦b:vellem scrīpsisset⟧, ⟦i:I wish he had written⟧.
2. With expressions of ⟦i:fearing⟧ (⟦b:timeō⟧, ⟦b:metuō⟧, ⟦b:vereor⟧, ⟦b:etc.⟧). Here ⟦b:nē⟧ means ⟦i:that⟧, ⟦i:lest⟧, and ⟦b:ut⟧ means ⟦i:that not⟧; as,—
⟦b:timeō nē veniat⟧, ⟦i:I fear that he will come⟧ (originally: ⟦i:may he not come! I'm afraid⟧ [⟦i:he will⟧]);
⟦b:timeō ut veniat⟧, ⟦i:I fear that he will not come⟧ (originally: ⟦i:may he come! I'm afraid⟧ [⟦i:he won't⟧]).
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Nē nōn⟧ sometimes occurs instead of ⟦b:ut⟧, especially where the verb of ⟦i:fearing⟧ has a negative, or where the writer desires to emphasize some particular word in the dependent clause; as,—
⟦b:nōn vereor ne hōc nōn fīat⟧, ⟦i:I am not afraid that this will not happen;⟧
⟦b:vereor nē exercitum fīrmum habēre nōn possit⟧, ⟦i:I fear that he is unable⟧ (⟦b:nōn possit⟧) ⟦i:to have a strong army.⟧
⟦i:C.⟧ Substantive Clauses of Result.
Substantive Clauses of Result (introduced by ⟦b:ut⟧, ⟦b:ut nōn⟧) are a development of pure Result clauses, and occur with the following classes of words:—
1. As object clauses after verbs of ⟦i:doing⟧, ⟦i:accomplishing⟧ (especially ⟦b:faciō⟧, ⟦b:efficiō⟧, ⟦b:cōnficiō⟧). Thus:—
⟦b:gravitās morbī facit ut medicīnā egeāmus⟧, ⟦i:the severity of disease makes us need medicine.⟧
2. As the subject of several impersonal verbs, particularly ⟦b:fit⟧, ⟦b:efficitur⟧, ⟦b:accidit⟧, ⟦b:ēvenit⟧, ⟦b:contingit⟧, ⟦b:accēdit⟧, ⟦b:fierī potest⟧, ⟦b:fore⟧, ⟦b:sequitur⟧, ⟦b:relinquitur⟧. Thus:—
⟦b:ex quō efficitur, ut voluptās nōn sit summum bonum⟧, ⟦i:from which it follows that pleasure is not the greatest good⟧;
⟦b:ita fit, ut nēmō esse possit beātus⟧, ⟦i:thus it happens that no one can be happy⟧;
⟦b:accēdēbat ut nāvēs deessent⟧, ⟦i:another thing was the lack of ships⟧ (lit. ⟦i:it was added that ships were lacking⟧).
3. As predicate or appositive after expressions like ⟦b:jūs est⟧, ⟦b:mōs est⟧, ⟦b:cōnsuētūdō est⟧; also after neuter pronouns, ⟦b:hōc⟧, ⟦b:illud⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧ Thus:—
⟦b:est mōs hominum ut nōlint eundem plūribus rēbus excellere⟧, ⟦i:it is the way of men not to wish the same person to excel in many things.⟧
⟦i:D.⟧ Substantive Clauses introduced by ⟦i:Quīn⟧.
Substantive Clauses introduced by ⟦b:quīn⟧ (used sometimes as subject, sometimes as object) occur after negative and interrogative expressions of ⟦i:doubt⟧, ⟦i:omission,⟧ and the like, particularly after ⟦b:nōn dubitō⟧, ⟦i:I do not doubt⟧; ⟦b:quis dubitat⟧, ⟦i:who doubts?⟧; ⟦b:nōn (haud) dubium est⟧, ⟦i:there is no doubt⟧. The mood is the Subjunctive. Examples:—
⟦b:quis dubitat quīn in virtūte dīvitiae sint⟧, ⟦i:who doubts that in virtue there are riches?⟧
⟦b:nōn dubium erat quīn ventūrus esset⟧, ⟦i:there was no doubt that he was about to come.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. In Nepos, Livy, and post-Augustan writers an Infinitive sometimes takes the place of the ⟦b:quīn⟧-clause after ⟦b:nōn dubitō⟧; as,—
⟦b:nōn dubitāmus inventōs esse⟧, ⟦i:we do not doubt that men were found⟧
⟦i:b⟧. ⟦b:Nōn dubitō⟧, ⟦i:I do not hesitate⟧, is regularly followed by the Infinitive, though sometimes by a ⟦b:quīn⟧-clause.
⟦i:E.⟧ Substantive Clauses Introduced by ⟦i:Quod⟧.
1. ⟦b:Quod⟧, ⟦i:the fact that⟧, ⟦i:that⟧, introduces Substantive Clauses in the Indicative. This construction occurs especially—
⟦i:a⟧) In apposition with a preceding demonstrative, as ⟦b:hōc⟧, ⟦b:id⟧, ⟦b:illud⟧, ⟦b:illa⟧, ⟦b:ex eō⟧, ⟦b:inde⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧ Thus:—
⟦b:illud est admīrātiōne dignum, quod captīvōs retinendōs cēnsuit⟧, ⟦i:this is especially worthy of admiration, that he thought the prisoners ought to be kept⟧;
⟦b:hōc ūnō praestāmus vel maximē ferīs, quod colloquimur inter nōs⟧, ⟦i:in this one respect we are especially superior to the beasts, that we talk with each other⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) After ⟦b:bene fit⟧, ⟦b:bene accidit⟧, ⟦b:male fit⟧, ⟦b:bene facere⟧, ⟦b:mīror⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; as,—
⟦b:bene mihi ēvenit, quod mittor ad mortem⟧, ⟦i:it is well for me that I am sent to death⟧;
⟦b:bene fēcistī quod mānsistī⟧, ⟦i:you did well in remaining.⟧
2. ⟦b:Quod⟧ at the beginning of the sentence sometimes has the force of ⟦i:as regards the fact that⟧. Thus:—
⟦b:quod multitūdinem Germānōrum in Galliam trādūcō, id meī mūniendī causā faciō⟧, ⟦i:as regards the fact that I am transporting a multitude of Germans into Gaul, I am doing it for the sake of strengthening myself;⟧
⟦b:quod mē Agamemnona aemulārī putās, falleris⟧, ⟦i:as regards your thinking that I emulate Agamemnon, you are mistaken⟧.
⟦i:F.⟧ Indirect Questions.
1. Indirect Questions are Substantive Clauses used after verbs of ⟦i:asking⟧, ⟦i:inquiring⟧, ⟦i:telling⟧, and the like. They take their verb in the Subjunctive. Like Direct Questions (see § 162) they may be introduced—
⟦i:a⟧) By Interrogative Pronouns or Adverbs; as,—
⟦b:dīc mihi ubi fuerīs, quid fēcerīs⟧, ⟦i:tell me where you were, what you did⟧;
⟦b:oculīs jūdicārī nōn potest in utram partem fluat Arar⟧, ⟦i:it cannot be determined by the eye in which direction the Arar flows⟧;
⟦b:bis bīna quot essent, nesciēbat⟧, ⟦i:he did not know how many two times two were⟧.
NOTE.—Care should be taken to distinguish Indirect Questions from Relative Clauses. The difference between the two appears clearly in the following:—
⟦b:effugere nēmō id potest quod futūrum est⟧, ⟦i:no one can escape what is destined to come to pass;⟧ but ⟦b:saepe autem ne ūtile quidem est scīre quid futūrum sit⟧, ⟦i:but often it is not even useful to know what is coming to pass.⟧
⟦i:b⟧) By ⟦b:num⟧ or ⟦b:-ne⟧, without distinction of meaning; as,—
⟦b:Epamīnōndās quaesīvit num salvus esset clipeus⟧, or ⟦b:salvusne esset clipeus⟧, ⟦i:Epaminondas asked whether his shield was safe⟧;
⟦b:disputātur num interīre virtūs in homine possit⟧, ⟦i:the question is raised whether virtue can die in a man⟧;
⟦b:ex Sōcrate quaesītum est nōnne Archelāum beātum putāret⟧, ⟦i:the question was asked of Socrates whether he did not think Archelaus happy⟧.
NOTE.—⟦b:Nōnne⟧ in Indirect Questions occurs only after ⟦b:quaerō⟧, as in the last example above.
2. Often the Indirect Question represents a Deliberative Subjunctive of the direct discourse; as,—
⟦b:nesciō quid faciam⟧, ⟦i:I do not know what to do.⟧ (Direct: ⟦b:quid faciam⟧, ⟦i:what shall I do!⟧)
3. After verbs of ⟦i:expectation⟧ and ⟦i:endeavor⟧ (⟦b:exspectō⟧, ⟦b:cōnor⟧, ⟦b:experior⟧, ⟦b:temptō⟧) we sometimes find an Indirect Question introduced by ⟦b:sī⟧; as,—
⟦b:cōnantur sī perrumpere possint⟧, ⟦i:they try whether they can break through.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. Sometimes the governing verb is omitted; as,—
⟦b:pergit ad proximam spēluncam sī forte eō vēstīgia ferrent⟧, ⟦i:he proceeded to the nearest cave (to see) if the tracks led thither.⟧
4. ⟦b:Indirect Double Questions⟧ are introduced in the main by the same particles as direct double questions (§ 162, 4); ⟦i:viz.⟧;—
⟦b:utrum ... an⟧;
⟦b:-ne ... an⟧;
⟦b:—— ... an⟧;
⟦b:—— ... ne⟧.
Examples:—
⟦b:quaerō utrum vērum an falsum sit⟧, ⟦b:quaerō vērumne an falsum sit⟧, ⟦b:quaerō vērum an falsum sit⟧, ⟦b:quaerō vērum falsumne sit⟧,  } } ⟦i:I ask whether it⟧ } ⟦i:is true or false?⟧ }
⟦/⟧
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦i:'Or not'⟧ in the second member of the double question is ordinarily expressed by ⟦b:necne⟧, less frequently by ⟦b:an nōn⟧; as,—
⟦b:dī utrum sint necne, quaeritur⟧, ⟦i:it is asked whether there are gods or not.⟧
5. ⟦b:Haud sciō an⟧, ⟦b:nesciō an⟧, by omission of the first member of the double question, occur with the Subjunctive in the sense: ⟦i:I am inclined to think, probably, perhaps;⟧ as,—
⟦b:haud sciō an ita sit⟧, ⟦i:I am inclined to think this is so.⟧
6. In early Latin and in poetry the Indicative is sometimes used in indirect Questions.

title: Conditional Sentences
text:
Conditional Sentences are compound sentences (§ 164) consisting of two parts, the Protasis (or ⟦i:condition⟧), usually introduced by ⟦b:sī⟧, ⟦b:nisi⟧, or ⟦b:sīn⟧, and the Apodosis (or ⟦i:conclusion⟧). There are the following types of Conditional Sentences:—
First Type.—Nothing Implied as to the Reality of the Supposed Case.
1. Here we regularly have the Indicative in both Protasis and Apodosis. Any tense may be used; as,—
⟦b:sī hōc crēdis, errās⟧, ⟦i:if you believe this, you are mistaken⟧;
⟦b:nātūram sī sequēmur, numquam aberrābimus⟧, ⟦i:if we follow Nature, we shall never go astray⟧;
⟦b:sī hōc dīxistī, errāstī⟧, ⟦i:if you said this, you were in error⟧.
2. Sometimes the Protasis takes the Indefinite Second Person Singular (§ 356, 3) of the Present or Perfect Subjunctive, with the force of the Indicative; as,—
⟦b:memoria minuitur, nisi eam exerceās⟧, ⟦i:memory is impaired unless you exercise it⟧.
3. Here belong also those conditional sentences in which the Protasis denotes a repeated action (compare §§ 287, 2; 288, 3); as,—
⟦b:sī quis equitum dēciderat, peditēs circumsistēbant⟧, ⟦i:if any one of the horsemen fell, the foot-soldiers gathered about him⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Instead of the Indicative, Livy and subsequent writers employ the Subjunctive of the Historical tenses in the Protasis to denote repeated action; as,—
⟦b:sī dīcendō quis diem eximeret⟧, ⟦i:if (ever) anybody consumed a day in pleading⟧; ⟦b:sī quandō adsidēret⟧, ⟦i:if ever he sat by⟧.
4. Where the sense demands it, the Apodosis in conditional sentences of the First Type may be an Imperative or one of the Independent Subjunctives (Hortatory, Deliberative, ⟦i:etc.⟧); as,—
⟦b:sī hōc crēditis, tacēte⟧, ⟦i:if you believe this, be silent⟧;
⟦b:sī hōc crēdimus, taceāmus⟧, ⟦i:if we believe this, let us keep silent⟧.
Second Type.—'Should'-'Would' Conditions.
Here we regularly have the Subjunctive (of the Present or Perfect tense) in both Protasis and Apodosis; as,—
⟦b:sī hōc dīcās, errēs⟧, or ⟦b:sī hōc dīxerīs, errāverīs⟧, ⟦i:if you should say this, you would be mistaken⟧;
⟦b:sī velim Hannibalis proelia omnia dēscrībere, diēs mē dēficiat⟧, ⟦i:if I should wish to describe all the battles of Hannibal, time would fail me⟧;
⟦b:mentiar, sī negem⟧, ⟦i:I should lie, if I should deny it⟧;
⟦b:haec sī tēcum patria loquātur, nōnne impetrāre dēbeat⟧, ⟦i:if your country should plead thus with you, would she not deserve to obtain her request?⟧
⟦i:a⟧. The Subjunctive in the Apodosis of conditional sentences of this type is of the Potential variety.
⟦i:b⟧. Sometimes we find the Indicative in the Apodosis of sentences of the Second Type, where the writer wishes to assert the accomplishment of a result more positively; as,—
⟦b:aliter sī faciat, nūllam habet auctōritātem⟧, ⟦i:if he should do otherwise, he has no authority⟧.
Third Type.—Supposed Case Represented as Contrary to Fact.
1. Here we regularly have the Subjunctive in both Protasis and Apodosis, the Imperfect referring ⟦i:to present time⟧, and the Pluperfect referring ⟦i:to past⟧; as,—
⟦b:sī amīcī meī adessent, opis nōn indigērem⟧, ⟦i:if my friends were here, I should not lack assistance⟧;
⟦b:sī hōc dīxissēs, errāssēs⟧, ⟦i:if you had said this, you would have erred⟧;
⟦b:sapientia nōn expeterētur, sī nihil efficeret⟧, ⟦i:philosophy would not be desired, if it accomplished nothing⟧;
⟦b:cōnsilium, ratiō, sententia nisi essent in senibus, nōn summum cōnsilium majōrēs nostrī appellāssent senātum⟧, ⟦i:unless deliberation, reason, and wisdom existed in old men, our ancestors would not have called their highest deliberative body a senate⟧.
2. Sometimes the Imperfect Subjunctive is found referring to the past, especially to denote ⟦i:a continued act, or a state of things still existing⟧; as,—
⟦b:Laelius, Fūrius, Catō sī nihil litterīs adjuvārentur, numquam sē ad eārum studium contulissent⟧, ⟦i:Laelius, Furius, and Cato would never have devoted themselves to the study of letters, unless they had been (constantly) helped by them⟧;
⟦b:num igitur sī ad centēsimum annum vīxisset, senectūtis eum suae paenitēret⟧, ⟦i:if he had lived to his hundredth year, would he have regretted (and now be regretting) his old age?⟧
3. The Apodosis in conditional sentences of this type sometimes stands in the Indicative (Imperfect, Perfect, or Pluperfect), ⟦i:viz.⟧—
⟦i:a⟧) Frequently in expressions of ⟦i:ability⟧, ⟦i:obligation⟧, or ⟦i:necessity⟧; as,—
⟦b:nisi fēlīcitās in sōcordiam vertisset, exuere jugum potuērunt⟧, ⟦i:unless their prosperity had turned to folly, they could have thrown off the yoke⟧;
NOTE.—In sentences of this type, however, it is not the ⟦i:possibility⟧ that is represented as-contrary-to-fact, but something to be supplied in thought from the context. Thus in the foregoing sentence the logical apodosis is ⟦i:et exuissent⟧ understood (⟦i:and they would have shaken it off⟧). When the ⟦i:possibility⟧ itself is conditioned, the Subjunctive is used.
⟦b:eum patris locō colere dēbēbās, sī ūlla in tē pietās esset⟧, ⟦i:you ought to revere him as a father, if you had any sense of devotion⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) With both the Periphrastic Conjugations; as,—
⟦b:sī Sēstius occīsus esset, fuistisne ad arma itūrī⟧, ⟦i:if Sestius had been slain, would you have proceeded to arms?⟧
⟦b:sī ūnum diem morātī essētis, moriendum omnibus fuit,⟧ ⟦i:if you had delayed one day, you would all have had to die⟧.
Protasis expressed without ⟦i:Sī⟧.
1. The Protasis is not always expressed by a clause with ⟦b:sī⟧, but may be implied in a word, a phrase, or merely by the context; as,—
⟦b:aliōquī haec nōn scrīberentur⟧, ⟦i:otherwise⟧ (⟦i:i.e.⟧ if matters were otherwise) ⟦i:these things would not be written⟧;
⟦b:nōn potestis, voluptāte omnia dīrigentēs, retinēre virtūtem⟧, ⟦i:you cannot retain virtue, if you direct everything with reference to pleasure⟧.
2. Sometimes an Imperative, or a Jussive Subjunctive, serves as Protasis. Thus:—
⟦b:crās petitō, dabitur⟧, ⟦i:if you ask to-morrow, it shall be given you⟧ (lit. ⟦i:ask to-morrow⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧);
⟦b:haec reputent, vidēbunt⟧, ⟦i:if they consider this, they will see⟧ (lit. ⟦i:let them consider⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧);
⟦b:rogēs Zēnōnem, respondeat⟧, ⟦i:if you should ask Zeno, he would answer⟧.
Use of ⟦i:Nisi⟧, ⟦i:Sī Nōn⟧, ⟦i:Sīn⟧.
1. ⟦b:Nisi⟧, ⟦i:unless⟧, negatives the entire protasis; ⟦b:sī nōn⟧ negatives a single word; as,—
⟦b:ferreus essem, nisi tē amārem⟧, ⟦i:I should be hard-hearted unless I loved you⟧; but—
⟦b:ferreus essem, sī tē nōn amārem⟧, ⟦i:I should be hard-hearted if I did⟧ NOT ⟦i:love you⟧.
In the first example, it is the notion of ⟦i:loving you⟧ that is negatived, in the second, the notion of ⟦i:loving⟧.
2. ⟦b:Sī nōn⟧ (⟦b:sī minus⟧) is regularly employed:—
⟦i:a⟧) When an apodosis with ⟦b:at⟧, ⟦b:tamen⟧, ⟦b:certē⟧ follows; as,—
⟦b:dolōrem sī nōn potuerō frangere, tamen occultābō⟧, ⟦i:if I cannot crush my sorrow, yet I will hide it.⟧
⟦i:b⟧) When an affirmative protasis is repeated in negative form; as,—
⟦b:sī fēceris, magnam habēbō grātiam; sī nōn fēceris, ignōscam⟧, ⟦i:if you do it, I shall be deeply grateful; if you do not do it, I shall pardon you⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. But if the verb is omitted in the repetition, only ⟦b:si minus⟧ or ⟦b:sin minus⟧ is admissible; as,—
⟦b:hōc sī assecūtus sum, gaudeō; sī minus, mē cōnsōlor⟧, ⟦i:if I have attained this, I am glad; if not, I console myself⟧.
3. ⟦b:Sīn⟧. Where one protasis is followed by another opposed in meaning, but affirmative in form, the second is introduced by ⟦b:sīn⟧; as,—
⟦b:hunc mihi timōrem ēripe; sī vērus est, nē opprimar, sīn falsus, ut timēre dēsinam⟧, ⟦i:relieve me of this fear; if it is well founded, that I may not be destroyed; but if it is groundless, that I may cease to fear⟧.
4. ⟦b:Nisi⟧ has a fondness for combining with negatives (⟦b:nōn⟧, ⟦b:nēmō⟧, ⟦b:nihil⟧); as,—
⟦b:nihil cōgitāvit nisi caedem⟧, ⟦i:he had no thought but murder⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Nōn⟧ and ⟦b:nisi⟧ are always separated in the best Latinity.
5. ⟦b:Nisi forte⟧, ⟦b:nisi vērō⟧, ⟦b:nisi sī⟧, ⟦i:unless perchance, unless indeed⟧ (often with ironical force), take the Indicative; as,—
⟦b:nisi vērō, quia perfecta rēs nōn est, nōn vidētur pūnienda⟧, ⟦i:unless indeed, because an act is not consummated, it does not seem to merit punishment⟧.
Conditional Clauses of Comparison.
1. Conditional Clauses of Comparison are introduced by the particles, ⟦b:ac sī⟧, ⟦b:ut sī⟧, ⟦b:quasi⟧, ⟦b:quam sī⟧, ⟦b:tamquam sī⟧, ⟦b:velut sī⟧, or simply by ⟦b:velut⟧ or ⟦b:tamquam⟧. They stand in the Subjunctive mood and regularly involve an ellipsis (see § 374, 1), as indicated in the following examples:—
⟦b:tantus patrēs metus cēpit, velut sī jam ad portās hostis esset⟧, ⟦i:as great fear seized the senators as (would have seized them) if the enemy were already at the gates⟧;
⟦b:sed quid ego hīs testibus ūtor quasi rēs dubia aut obscūra sit⟧, ⟦i:but why do I use these witnesses, as (I should do) if the matter were doubtful or obscure⟧;
⟦b:serviam tibi tam quasi ēmerīs mē argentō⟧, ⟦i:I will serve you as though you had bought me for money⟧.
2. Note that in sentences of this kind the Latin observes the regular principles for the Sequence of Tenses. Thus after principal tenses the Latin uses the Present and Perfect (as in the second and third examples), where the English uses the Past and Past Perfect.
Concessive Clauses.
The term 'Concessive' is best restricted to those clauses developed from the Jussive Subjunctive which have the force of ⟦i:granted that⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; (see § 278) as,—
⟦b:sit fūr, sit sacrilegus, at est bonus imperātor⟧, ⟦i:granted that he is a thief and a robber, yet he is a good commander⟧;
⟦b:haec sint falsa⟧, ⟦i:granted that this is false⟧;
⟦b:nē sit summum malum dolor, malum certē est⟧, ⟦i:granted that pain is not the greatest evil, yet it is certainly an evil⟧.
Adversative Clauses with ⟦i:Quamvīs⟧, ⟦i:Quamquam⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧
Clauses introduced by ⟦b:quamvīs⟧, ⟦b:quamquam⟧, ⟦b:etsī⟧, ⟦b:tametsī⟧, ⟦b:cum⟧, ⟦i:although⟧, while often classed as 'Concessive,' are yet essentially different from genuine Concessive clauses. As a rule, they do not ⟦i:grant⟧ or ⟦i:concede⟧ anything, but rather state that something is true ⟦i:in spite of something else⟧. They accordingly emphasize the adversative idea, and are properly Subordinate Adversative Clauses. The different particles used to introduce these clauses have different meanings and take different constructions, as follows:—
1. ⟦b:Quamvīs⟧, ⟦i:however much⟧, ⟦i:although⟧, does not introduce a statement of fact, but represents an act merely as conceived. It is followed by the Subjunctive, usually of the present tense; as,—
⟦b:hominēs quamvīs in turbidīs rēbus sint, tamen interdum animīs relaxantur⟧, ⟦i:in however stirring events men may engage, yet at times they relax their energies;⟧
⟦b:nōn est potestās opitulandī reī pūblicae quamvīs ea premātur perīculīs⟧, ⟦i:there is no opportunity to succor the state, though it be beset by dangers.⟧
2. ⟦b:Quamquam⟧, ⟦b:etsī⟧, ⟦b:tametsī⟧, ⟦i:although⟧, introduce a statement of fact, and are followed by the Indicative (of any tense); as,—
