⟦b:quamquam omnis virtūs nōs allicit, tamen jūstitia id maximē efficit⟧, ⟦i:although all virtue attracts us, yet justice does so especially;⟧
⟦b:Caesar, etsī nōndum cōnsilium hostium cognōverat, tamen id quod accidit suspicābātur⟧, ⟦i:Caesar, though he did not yet know the plans of the enemy, yet was suspecting what actually occurred⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Etsī⟧, ⟦i:although⟧, must be distinguished from ⟦b:etsī⟧, ⟦i:even if⟧. The latter is a conditional particle and takes any of the constructions admissible for ⟦b:sī⟧. (See §§ 302-304.)
3. ⟦b:Cum⟧, ⟦i:although⟧, is followed by the Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:Atticus honōrēs nōn petiit, cum eī patērent⟧, ⟦i:Atticus did not seek honors, though they were open to him⟧.
4. ⟦b:Licet⟧ sometimes loses its verbal force (see § 295, 6) and sinks to the level of a conjunction with the force of ⟦i:although⟧. It takes the Subjunctive, Present or Perfect; as,—
⟦b:licet omnēs terrōrēs impendeant, succurram⟧, ⟦i:though all terrors hang over me, (yet) I will lend aid⟧.
5. ⟦b:Quamquam⟧, with the force ⟦i:and yet⟧, is often used to introduce principal clauses; as,—
⟦b:quamquam quid loquor⟧, ⟦i:and yet why do I speak?⟧
6. In post-Augustan writers ⟦b:quamquam⟧ is freely construed with the Subjunctive, while ⟦b:quamvīs⟧ is often used to introduce statements of fact, and takes either the Indicative or the Subjunctive. Thus:—
⟦b:quamquam movērētur hīs vōcibus⟧, ⟦i:although he was moved by these words⟧;
⟦b:quamvīs multī opīnārentur⟧, ⟦i:though many thought⟧;
⟦b:quamvīs īnfēstō animō pervēnerās⟧, ⟦i:though you had come with hostile intent⟧.
Clauses with ⟦i:Dum⟧, ⟦i:Modo⟧, ⟦i:Dummodo⟧, denoting a Wish or a Proviso.
These particles are followed by the Subjunctive (negative ⟦b:nē⟧) and have two distinct uses:—
I. They are used to introduce clauses ⟦i:embodying a wish⟧ entertained by the subject of the leading verb; as,—
⟦b:multī honesta neglegunt dummodo potentiam cōnsequantur⟧, ⟦i:many neglect honor in their desire to obtain power⟧ (⟦i:if only they may attain⟧);
⟦b:omnia postposuī, dum praeceptīs patris pārērem⟧, ⟦i:I made everything else secondary, in my desire to obey the injunctions of my father⟧;
⟦b:nīl obstat tibi, dum nē sit dītior alter⟧, ⟦i:nothing hinders you in your desire that your neighbor may not be richer than you⟧.
II. They are used to express a ⟦i:proviso⟧ ('⟦i:provided that⟧'); as,—
⟦b:ōderint, dum metuant⟧, ⟦i:let them hate, provided they fear⟧;
⟦b:manent ingenia senibus, modo permaneat studium et industria⟧, ⟦i:old men retain their faculties, provided only they retain their interest and vigor⟧;
⟦b:nūbant, dum nē dōs fiat comes⟧, ⟦i:let them marry, provided no dowry goes with it⟧.
Relative Clauses.
Relative Clauses are introduced by Relative Pronouns, Adjectives, or Adverbs.
1. Relative clauses usually stand in the Indicative Mood, especially clauses introduced by those General Relatives which are doubled or have the suffix ⟦b:-oumque⟧; as,—
⟦b:quidquid id est, timeō Danaōs et dōna ferentēs⟧, ⟦i:whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when they offer gifts;⟧
⟦b:quidquid oritur, quālecumque est, causam ā nātūrā habet⟧, ⟦i:whatever comes into being, of whatever sort it is, has its primal cause in Nature.⟧
2. Any simple Relative may introduce a conditional sentence of any of the three types mentioned in §§ 302-304; as,—
⟦b:quī hōc dīcit, errat⟧, ⟦i:he who says this is mistaken⟧ (First Type);
⟦b:quī hōc dīcat, erret⟧, ⟦i:he would be mistaken who should say this⟧ (Second Type);
⟦b:quī hōc dīxisset, errāsset⟧, ⟦i:the man who had said this would have been mistaken.⟧

title: Indirect Discourse (Ōrātiō Oblīqua)
text:
When the language or thought of any person is reproduced without change, that is called Direct Discourse (⟦i:Ōrātiō Recta⟧); as, ⟦i:Caesar said, 'The die is cast.'⟧ When, on the other hand, one's language or thought is made to depend upon a verb of ⟦i:saying⟧, ⟦i:thinking⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧, that is called Indirect Discourse (⟦i:Ōrātiō Oblīqua⟧); as, ⟦i:Caesar said that the die was cast; Caesar thought that his troops were victorious.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. For the verbs most frequently employed to introduce Indirect Discourse, see § 331.
Declarative Sentences.

title: Moods in Indirect Discourse
text:
1. Declarative Sentences upon becoming Indirect change their main clause to the Infinitive with Subject Accusative, while all subordinate clauses take the Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:Rēgulus dīxit quam diū jūre jūrandō hostium tenērētur nōn esse sē senātōrem⟧, ⟦i:Regulus said that as long as he was held by his pledge to the enemy he was not a senator.⟧ (Direct: ⟦b:quam diū teneor nōn sum senātor.⟧)
2. The verb of ⟦i:saying⟧, ⟦i:thinking⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧, is sometimes to be inferred from the context; as,—
⟦b:tum Rōmulus lēgātōs circā vīcīnās gentēs mīsit quī societātem cōnūbiumque peterent: urbēs quoque, ut cētera, ex īnfimō nāscī⟧, ⟦i:then Romulus sent envoys around among the neighboring tribes, to ask for alliance and the right of intermarriage, (saying that) cities, like everything else, start from a modest beginning⟧.
3. Subordinate clauses which contain an explanatory statement of the writer and so are not properly a part of the Indirect Discourse, or which emphasize the fact stated, take the Indicative; as,—
⟦b:nūntiātum est Ariovistum ad occupandum Vesontiōnem, quod est oppidum maximum Sēquanōrum contendere⟧, ⟦i:it was reported that Ariovistus was hastening to seize Vesontio, which is the largest town of the Sequani⟧.
4. Sometimes a subordinate clause is such only in its external form, and in sense is principal. It then takes the Infinitive with Subject Accusative. This occurs especially in case of relative clauses, where quī is equivalent to ⟦b:et hīc⟧, ⟦b:nam hīc⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; as,—
⟦b:dīxit urbem Athēniēnsium prōpugnāculum oppositum esse barbarīs, apud quam jam bis classēs rēgiās fēcisse naufragium⟧, ⟦i:he said the city of the Athenians had been set against the barbarians like a bulwark, near which (= and near it) the fleets of the King had twice met disaster⟧.
5. The Subject Accusative of the Infinitive is sometimes omitted when it refers to the same person as the subject of the leading verb, or can easily be supplied from the context; as,—
⟦b:cum id nescīre Māgō dīceret⟧, ⟦i:when Mago said he did not know this⟧ (for ⟦b:sē nescīre⟧).
Interrogative Sentences.
1. Real questions of the Direct Discourse, upon becoming indirect, are regularly put in the Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:Ariovistus Caesarī respondit: sē prius in Galliam vēnisse quam populum Rōmānum. Quid sibi vellet? Cūr in suās possessiōnēs venīret⟧, ⟦i:Ariovistus replied to Caesar that he had come into Gaul before the Roman people. What did he (Caesar) mean? Why did he come into his domain?⟧ (Direct: ⟦b:quid tibi vīs? cūr in meās possessiōnēs venīs?⟧)
2. Rhetorical questions, on the other hand, being asked merely for effect, and being equivalent in force to emphatic statements, regularly stand in the Infinitive in Indirect Discourse. Thus :—
⟦b:quid est levius⟧ (lit. ⟦i:what is more trivial⟧, = nothing is more trivial) of the Direct Discourse becomes ⟦b:quid esse levius⟧ in the Indirect.
3. Deliberative Subjunctives of the Direct Discourse remain unchanged in mood in the Indirect: as,—
⟦b:quid faceret⟧, ⟦i:what was he to do?⟧ (Direct: ⟦b:quid faciat?⟧)
Imperative Sentences.
All Imperatives or Jussive Subjunctives of the Direct Discourse appear as Subjunctives in the Indirect; as,—
⟦b:mīlitēs certiōrēs fēcit paulisper intermitterent proelium⟧, ⟦i:he told the soldiers to stop the battle for a little⟧. (Direct: ⟦b:intermittite.⟧)
⟦i:a⟧. The negative in such sentences is ⟦b:nē⟧; as,—
⟦b:nē suae virtūtī tribueret⟧, ⟦i:let him not attribute it to his own valor!⟧
⟦i:A.⟧ Tenses of the Infinitive.

title: Tenses in Indirect Discourse
text:
These are used in accordance with the regular principles for the use of the Infinitive as given in § 270.
⟦i:a⟧. The Perfect Infinitive may represent any past tense of the Indicative of Direct Discourse. Thus:—
⟦b:sciō tē haec ēgisse⟧ may mean—
⟦i:I know you were doing this⟧.(Direct: ⟦b:haec agēbās⟧.)
⟦i:I know you did this⟧. (Direct: ⟦b:haec ēgistī⟧.)
⟦i:I know you had done this⟧. (Direct: ⟦b:haec ēgerās⟧.)
⟦i:B.⟧ Tenses of the Subjunctive.
These follow the regular principle for the Sequence of Tenses, being Principal if the verb of ⟦i:saying⟧ is Principal; Historical if it is Historical. Yet for the sake of vividness, we often find the Present Subjunctive used after an historical tense (⟦i:Repraesentātiō⟧); as,—
⟦b:Caesar respondit, sī obsidēs dentur, sēsē pācem esse factūrum⟧, ⟦i:Caesar replied that, if hostages be given, he would make peace⟧.
a. For the sequence after the Perfect Infinitive, see § 268, 2.
Conditional Sentences of the First Type.

title: Conditional Sentences in Indirect Discourse
text:
⟦i:A.⟧ THE APODOSIS. Any tense of the Indicative is changed to the corresponding tense of the Infinitive (§§ 270; 317, ⟦i:a⟧).
⟦i:B.⟧ THE PROTASIS. The protasis takes those tenses of the Subjunctive which are required by the Sequence of Tenses.
Examples:—
DIRECT.  INDIRECT.
sī hōc ⟦b:crēdis, errās⟧,  dīcō, sī hōc ⟦b:crēdās⟧, tē ⟦b:errāre⟧; dīxī, sī hōc ⟦b:crēderēs⟧, tē ⟦b:errāre⟧.
sī hōc ⟦b:crēdēs, errābis⟧,  dīcō, sī hōc ⟦b:crēdās⟧, tē ⟦b:errātūrum esse⟧; dīxī, sī hōc ⟦b:crēderēs⟧, tē ⟦b:errātūrum esse⟧.
sī hōc ⟦b:crēdideris, errābis⟧,  dīcō, sī hōc ⟦b:crēderīs⟧, tē ⟦b:errātūrum esse⟧; dīxī, sī hōc ⟦b:crēdidissēs⟧, tē ⟦b:errātūrum esse⟧.
sī hōc ⟦b:crēdēbās, errāvistī⟧,  dīcō, sī hōc ⟦b:crēderēs⟧, tē ⟦b:errāvisse⟧; dīxī, sī hōc ⟦b:crēderēs⟧, tē ⟦b:errāvisse⟧.
⟦/⟧
⟦i:a⟧. Note that a Future Perfect Indicative of the Direct Discourse regularly appears in the Indirect as a Perfect Subjunctive after a principal tense, and as a Pluperfect Subjunctive after an historical tense.
Conditional Sentences of the Second Type.
⟦i:A.⟧ THE APODOSIS. The Present Subjunctive of the Direct Discourse regularly becomes the Future Infinitive of the Indirect.
⟦i:B.⟧ THE PROTASIS. The Protasis takes those tenses of the Subjunctive demanded by the sequence of tenses.
Examples:—
sī hōc ⟦b:crēdās, errēs⟧,  dīcō, sī hōc ⟦b:crēdās⟧, tē ⟦b:errātūrum esse⟧; dīxī, sī hōc ⟦b:crēderēs⟧, tē ⟦b:errātūrum esse⟧;
⟦/⟧
Conditional Sentences of the Third Type.
⟦i:A.⟧ THE APODOSIS.
1. The Imperfect Subjunctive of the Direct Discourse becomes the Future Infinitive.
⟦i:a⟧. But this construction is rare, being represented in the classical Latinity by a single example (Caesar, V. 29. 2). Some scholars question the correctness of this passage.
2. The Pluperfect Subjunctive of the Direct Discourse becomes:—
⟦i:a⟧) In the Active Voice the Infinitive in ⟦b:-ūrus fuisse⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) In the Passive Voice it takes the form ⟦b:futūrum fuisse ut⟧ with the Imperfect Subjunctive.
⟦i:B.⟧ THE PROTASIS. The protasis in Conditional Sentences of this type always remains unchanged.
Examples:—
sī hōc ⟦b:crēderēs, errārēs⟧,  dīcō (dīxī), sī hōc ⟦b:crēderēs, tē errātūrum esse⟧;
sī hōc ⟦b:crēdidissēs, errāvissēs⟧,  dīcō (dīxī), sī hōc ⟦b:crēdidissēs, tē errātūrum fuisse⟧;
sī hōc ⟦b:dīxissēs, pūnītus essēs⟧.  dīcō (dīxī), sī hōc ⟦b:dīxissēs, futūrum fuisse ut pūnīrēris⟧.
⟦/⟧
When an apodosis of a conditional sentence of the Third Type referring to the past is at the same time a Result clause or a ⟦b:quīn⟧-clause (after ⟦b:nōn dubitō⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧), it stands in the Perfect Subjunctive in the form ⟦b:-ūrus fuerim⟧; as,—
⟦b:ita territī sunt, ut arma trāditūrī fuerint, nisi Caesar subitō advēnisset⟧, ⟦i:they were so frightened that they would have given up their arms, had not Caesar suddenly arrived⟧;
⟦b:nōn dubitō quīn, sī hōc dīxissēs, errātūrus fuerīs⟧,[57] ⟦i:I do not doubt that, if you had said this, you would have made a mistake⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. This peculiarity is confined to the Active Voice. In the Passive, such sentences, when they become dependent, remain unchanged; as,—
⟦b:nōn dubitō quīn, sī hōc dīxissēs, vituperātus essēs⟧, ⟦i:I do not doubt that, if you had said this, you would have been blamed⟧.
⟦i:b⟧. When an Indirect Question becomes an apodosis in a conditional sentence of the Third Type, ⟦b:-ūrus fuerim⟧ (rarely ⟦b:-ūrus fuissem⟧) is used; as,—
⟦b:quaerō, num, sī hōc dīxissēs, errātūrus fuerīs⟧ (or ⟦b:fuissēs⟧).
⟦i:c⟧. ⟦b:Potuī⟧, when it becomes a dependent apodosis in sentences of this Type, usually changes to the Perfect Subjunctive; as,—
⟦b:concursū tōtīus civitātis dēfēnsī sunt, ut frīgidissimōs quoque ōrātōrēs populī studia excitāre potuerint,⟧ ⟦i:they were defended before a gathering of all the citizens, so that the interest of the people would have been enough to excite even the most apathetic orators⟧.

title: Implied Indirect Discourse
Subjunctive by Attraction
The Infinitive
text:
This is used chiefly as Subject or Object but also as Predicate or Appositive.
NOTE.—The Infinitive was originally a Dative, and traces of this are still to be seen in the poetical use of the Infinitive to express ⟦i:purpose⟧; as, ⟦b:nec dulcēs occurrent ōscula nātī praeripere⟧, ⟦i:and no sweet children will run to snatch kisses⟧.
⟦i:A. As Subject.⟧
1. The Infinitive without Subject Accusative is used as the Subject of ⟦b:esse⟧ and various impersonal verbs, particularly ⟦b:opus est⟧, ⟦b:necesse est⟧, ⟦b:oportet⟧, ⟦b:juvat⟧, ⟦b:dēlectat⟧, ⟦b:placet⟧, ⟦b:libet⟧, ⟦b:licet⟧, ⟦b:praestat⟧, ⟦b:decet⟧, ⟦b:pudet⟧, ⟦b:interest⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; as,—
⟦b:dulce et decōrum est prō patriā morī⟧, ⟦i:it is sweet and noble to die for one's country⟧;
⟦b:virōrum est fortium toleranter dolōrem patī⟧, ⟦i:it is the part of brave men to endure pain with patience⟧;
⟦b:senātuī placuit lēgātōs mittere⟧, ⟦i:the Senate decided⟧ (lit. ⟦i:it pleased the Senate⟧) ⟦i:to send envoys⟧.
2. Even though the Infinitive itself appears without Subject, it may take a Predicate Noun or Adjective in the Accusative; as,—
⟦b:aliud est īrācundum esse, aliud īrātum⟧, ⟦i:it is one thing to be irascible, another to be angry⟧;
⟦b:impūne quaelibet facere, id est rēgem esse⟧, ⟦i:to do whatever you please with impunity, that is to be a king⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. But when ⟦b:licet⟧ is followed by a Dative of the person, a Predicate Noun or Adjective with ⟦b:esse⟧ is attracted into the same case; as, ⟦b:licuit esse ōtiōsō Themistoclī⟧, lit. ⟦i:it was permitted to Themistocles to be at leisure⟧. So sometimes with other Impersonals.
⟦i:B. As Object.⟧
1. The Infinitive without Subject Accusative is used as the Object of many verbs, to denote another action of the same subject, particularly after—
⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:cupiō⟧, ⟦b:mālō⟧, ⟦b:nōlō⟧, ⟦b:dēbeo⟧, ⟦i:ought⟧; ⟦b:statuō⟧, ⟦b:cōnstituō⟧, ⟦i:decide⟧; ⟦b:audeō⟧, ⟦i:dare⟧; ⟦b:studeō⟧, ⟦b:contendō⟧, ⟦i:strive⟧; ⟦b:parō⟧, ⟦i:prepare⟧ (so ⟦b:parātus⟧); ⟦b:incipiō⟧, ⟦b:coepī⟧, ⟦b:īnstituō⟧, ⟦i:begin⟧; ⟦b:pergō⟧, ⟦i:continue⟧; ⟦b:dēsinō⟧, ⟦b:dēsistō⟧, ⟦i:cease⟧; ⟦b:possum⟧, ⟦i:can⟧; ⟦b:cōnor⟧, ⟦i:try⟧;  ⟦b:cōgitō⟧, ⟦b:meditor⟧, ⟦i:purpose⟧, ⟦i:intend⟧; ⟦b:neglegō⟧, ⟦i:neglect⟧; ⟦b:vereor⟧, ⟦b:timeō⟧, ⟦i:fear⟧; ⟦b:mātūrō⟧, ⟦b:festīnō⟧, ⟦b:properō⟧, ⟦b:contendō⟧, ⟦i:hasten⟧; ⟦b:assuēscō⟧, ⟦b:cōnsuēscō⟧, ⟦i:accustom myself⟧ (so ⟦b:assuētus⟧, ⟦b:īnsuētus⟧, ⟦b:assuēfactus⟧); ⟦b:discō⟧, ⟦i:learn⟧; ⟦b:sciō⟧, ⟦i:know how⟧; ⟦b:soleō⟧, ⟦i:am wont⟧;
⟦/⟧
as,—
⟦b:tū hōs intuērī audēs⟧, ⟦i:do you dare to look on these men⟧?
⟦b:Dēmosthenēs ad flūctūs maris dēclāmāre solēbat⟧, ⟦i:Demosthenes used to declaim by the waves of the sea⟧.
2. A Predicate Noun or Adjective with these Infinitives is attracted into the Nominative; as,—
⟦b:beātus esse sine virtūte nēmō potest⟧, ⟦i:no one can be happy without virtue⟧;
⟦b:Catō esse quam vidērī bonus mālēbat⟧, ⟦i:Cato preferred to be good rather than to seem so⟧.
Infinitive with Subject Accusative.
This is used chiefly as Subject or Object but also as Predicate or Appositive.
⟦i:A. As Subject.⟧
The Infinitive with Subject Accusative (like the simple Infinitive) is used as Subject with ⟦b:esse⟧ and Impersonal verbs, particularly with ⟦b:aequum est⟧, ⟦b:ūtile est⟧, ⟦b:turpe est⟧, ⟦b:fāma est⟧, ⟦b:spēs est⟧, ⟦b:fās est⟧, ⟦b:nefās est⟧, ⟦b:opus est⟧, ⟦b:necesse est⟧, ⟦b:oportet⟧, ⟦b:cōnstat⟧, ⟦b:praestat⟧, ⟦b:licet⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; as,—
⟦b:nihil in bellō oportet contemnī⟧, ⟦i:nothing ought to be despised in war⟧;
⟦b:apertum est sibi quemque nātūrā esse cārum⟧, ⟦i:it is manifest that by nature everybody is dear to himself⟧.
⟦i:B. As Object.⟧
The Infinitive with Subject Accusative is used as Object after the following classes of verbs:
1. Most frequently after verbs of ⟦i:saying⟧, ⟦i:thinking⟧, ⟦i:knowing⟧, ⟦i:perceiving⟧, and the like (⟦i:Verba Sentiendi et Dēclārandī⟧). This is the regular construction of Principal Clauses of Indirect Discourse. Verbs that take this construction are, among others, the following: ⟦b:sentiō⟧, ⟦b:audiō⟧, ⟦b:videō⟧, ⟦b:cognōscō⟧; ⟦b:putō⟧, ⟦b:jūdicō⟧, ⟦b:spērō⟧, ⟦b:cōnfīdō⟧; ⟦b:sciō⟧, ⟦b:meminī⟧; ⟦b:dicō⟧, ⟦b:affīrmō⟧, ⟦b:negō⟧ (⟦i:say that ... not⟧), ⟦b:trādō⟧, ⟦b:nārrō⟧, ⟦b:fateor⟧, ⟦b:respondeō⟧, ⟦b:scrībō⟧, ⟦b:prōmittō⟧, ⟦b:glōrior⟧. Also the phrases: ⟦b:certiōrem faciō⟧ (⟦i:inform⟧), ⟦b:memoriā teneō⟧ (⟦i:remember⟧), ⟦i:etc.⟧
Examples:—
⟦b:Epicūrēī putant cum corporibus simul animōs interīre⟧, ⟦i:the Epicureans think that the soul perishes with the body⟧;
⟦b:Thalēs dīxit aquam esse initium rērum⟧, ⟦i:Thales said that water was the first principle of the universe⟧;
⟦b:Dēmocritus negat quicquid esse sempiternum⟧, ⟦i:Democritus says nothing is everlasting;⟧
⟦b:spērō eum ventūrum esse⟧, ⟦i:I hope that he will come⟧.
II. With ⟦b:jubeō⟧, ⟦i:order⟧, and ⟦b:vetō⟧, ⟦i:forbid⟧; as,—
⟦b:Caesar mīlitēs pontem facere jussit⟧, ⟦i:Caesar ordered the soldiers to make a bridge⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. When the name of the person who is ordered or forbidden to do something is omitted, the Infinitive with ⟦b:jubeō⟧ and ⟦b:vetō⟧ is put in the Passive; as, ⟦b:Caesar pontem fierī jussit⟧.
III. With ⟦b:patior⟧ and ⟦b:sinō⟧, ⟦i:permit⟧, ⟦i:allow⟧; as,—
⟦b:nūllō sē implicārī negōtiō passus est⟧, ⟦i:he did not permit himself to be involved in any difficulty⟧.
IV. With ⟦b:volō⟧, ⟦b:nōlō⟧, ⟦b:mālō⟧, ⟦b:cupiō⟧, when the Subject of the Infinitive is different from that of the governing verb; as,—
⟦b:nec mihi hunc errōrem extorquērī volō⟧, ⟦i:nor do I wish this error to be wrested from me⟧;
⟦b:eās rēs jactārī nōlēbat⟧, ⟦i:he was unwilling that these matters should be discussed⟧;
⟦b:tē tuā fruī virtūte cupimus⟧, ⟦i:we desire that you enjoy your worth⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. When the Subject of both verbs is the same, the simple Infinitive is regularly used in accordance with § 328, 1. But exceptions occur, especially in case of ⟦b:esse⟧ and Passive Infinitives as,—
⟦b:cupiō mē esse clēmentem⟧, ⟦i:I desire to be lenient⟧;
⟦b:Tīmoleōn māluit sē diligī quam metuī⟧, ⟦i:Timoleon preferred to be loved rather than feared⟧.
⟦i:b⟧. ⟦b:Volō⟧ also admits the Subjunctive, with or without ut; ⟦b:nōlō⟧ the Subjunctive alone. (See § 296, 1, ⟦i:a⟧.)
V. With Verbs of ⟦i:emotion⟧ (⟦i:joy⟧, ⟦i:sorrow⟧, ⟦i:regret⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧), especially ⟦b:gaudeō⟧, ⟦b:laetor⟧, ⟦b:doleō⟧; ⟦b:aegrē ferō⟧, ⟦b:molestē ferō⟧, ⟦b:graviter ferō⟧, ⟦i:am annoyed⟧, ⟦i:distressed⟧; ⟦b:mīror⟧, ⟦b:queror⟧, ⟦b:indignor⟧; as,—
⟦b:gaudeō tē salvum advenīre⟧, ⟦i:I rejoice that you arrive safely⟧;
⟦b:nōn molestē ferunt sē libīdinum vinculīs laxātōs ēsse⟧, ⟦i:they are not troubled at being released from the bonds of passion⟧;
⟦b:mīror tē ad mē nihil scrībere⟧, ⟦i:I wonder that you write me nothing⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Instead of an Infinitive these verbs also sometimes admit a ⟦b:quod-⟧ clause as Object. (See § 299.) Thus:—
⟦b:mīror quod nōn loqueris⟧, ⟦i:I wonder that you do not speak⟧.
VI. Some verbs which take two Accusatives, one of the Person and the other of the Thing (§ 178, 1), may substitute an Infinitive for the second Accusative; as,—
⟦b:cōgō tē hōc facere⟧, ⟦i:I compel you to do this⟧ (⟦i:cf.⟧ ⟦b:tē hōc cōgō⟧);
⟦b:docuī tē contentum esse⟧, ⟦i:I taught you to be content⟧ (⟦i:cf.⟧ ⟦b:tē modestiam docuī⟧, ⟦i:I taught you temperance⟧).
Passive Construction of the Foregoing Verbs.
Those verbs which in the Active are followed by the Infinitive with Subject Accusative, usually admit the personal construction of the Passive. This is true of the following and of some others:—
⟦i:a⟧) ⟦b:jubeor⟧, ⟦b:vetor⟧, ⟦b:sinor⟧; as,—
⟦b:mīlitēs pontem facere jussī sunt⟧, ⟦i:the soldiers were ordered to build a bridge⟧;
⟦b:pōns fierī jussus est⟧, ⟦i:a bridge was ordered built⟧;
⟦b:mīlitēs castrīs exīre vetitī sunt⟧, ⟦i:the troops were forbidden to go out of the camp⟧;
⟦b:Sēstius Clōdium accūsāre nōn est situs⟧, ⟦i:Sestius was not allowed to accuse Clodius⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) ⟦b:videor⟧, ⟦i:I am seen⟧, ⟦i:I seem⟧; as,—
⟦b:vidētur comperisse⟧, ⟦i:he seems to have discovered⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) ⟦b:dīcor⟧, ⟦b:putor⟧, ⟦b:exīstimor⟧, ⟦b:jūdicor⟧ (in all persons); as,—
⟦b:dīcitur in Italiam vēnisse⟧, ⟦i:he is said to have come into Italy⟧;
⟦b:Rōmulus prīmus rēx Rōmānōrum fuisse putātur⟧, ⟦i:Romulus is thought to have been the first king of the Romans⟧.
⟦i:d⟧) ⟦b:fertur⟧, ⟦b:feruntur⟧, ⟦b:trāditur⟧, ⟦b:trāduntur⟧ (only in the third person); as,—
⟦b:fertur Homērus caecus fuisse⟧, ⟦i:Homer is said to have been blind⟧;
⟦b:carmina Archilochī contumēliīs referta esse trāduntur,⟧ ⟦i:Archilochus's poems are reported to have been full of abuse⟧.
NOTE.—In compound tenses and periphrastic forms, the last two classes of verbs, ⟦i:c⟧), ⟦i:d⟧), more commonly take the impersonal construction; as—
⟦b:trāditum est Homērum caecum fuisse⟧, ⟦i:the story goes that Homer was blind⟧.
Infinitive with Adjectives.
The Infinitive with Adjectives (except ⟦b:parātus⟧, ⟦b:assuētus⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; see § 328, 1) occurs only in poetry and post-Augustan prose writers; as,—
⟦b:contentus dēmōnstrāsse⟧, ⟦i:contented to have proved⟧;
⟦b:audāx omnia perpetī⟧, ⟦i:bold for enduring everything⟧.
Infinitive in Exclamations.
The Infinitive is used in Exclamations implying ⟦i:scorn⟧, ⟦i:indignation⟧, or ⟦i:regret⟧. An intensive ⟦b:-ne⟧ is often attached to some word in the clause. Examples:—
⟦b:huncine sōlem tam nigrum surrēxe mihi⟧, ⟦i:to think that to-day's sun rose with such evil omen for me!⟧
⟦b:sedēre tōtōs diēs in vīllā⟧, ⟦i:to stay whole days at the villa⟧.
Historical Infinitive.
The Infinitive is often used in historical narrative instead of the Imperfect Indicative. The Subject stands in the Nominative; as,—
⟦b:interim cottīdiē Caesar Haeduōs frūmentum flāgitāre⟧, ⟦i:meanwhile Caesar was daily demanding grain of the Haedui⟧.
Tenses of the Participle.

title: Participles
text:
1. The tenses of the Participle, like those of the infinitive (see § 270), express time not absolutely, but with reference to the verb upon which the Participle depends.
2. The Present Participle denotes action ⟦i:contemporary with⟧ that of the verb. Thus:—
⟦b:audiō tē loquentem⟧ = ⟦i:you⟧ ARE ⟦i:speaking and I hear you⟧;
⟦b:audiēbam tē loquentem⟧ = ⟦i:you⟧ WERE ⟦i:speaking and I heard you⟧;
⟦b:audiam tē loquentem⟧ = ⟦i:you⟧ WILL BE ⟦i:speaking and I shall hear you.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. The Present Participle is sometimes employed with Conative force; as,—
⟦b:assurgentem rēgem resupīnat⟧, ⟦i:as the king was trying to rise, he threw him down.⟧
3. The Perfect Passive Participle denotes action ⟦i:prior to⟧ that of the verb. Thus:—
⟦b:locūtus taceō⟧ = ⟦i:I⟧ HAVE ⟦i:spoken and am silent⟧;
⟦b:locūtus tacui⟧ = ⟦i:I⟧ HAD ⟦i:spoken and then was silent⟧;
⟦b:locūtus tacēbō⟧ = ⟦i:I⟧ SHALL ⟦i:speak and then shall be silent.⟧
4. The absolute time of the action of a participle, therefore, is determined entirely by the finite verb with which it is connected.
5. Certain Perfect Passive Participles of Deponent and Semi-Deponent Verbs are used as Presents; ⟦i:viz.⟧ ⟦b:arbitrātus⟧, ⟦b:ausus⟧, ⟦b:ratus⟧, ⟦b:gāvīsus⟧, ⟦b:solitus⟧, ⟦b:ūsus⟧, ⟦b:cōnfīsus⟧, ⟦b:diffīsus⟧, ⟦b:secūtus⟧, ⟦b:veritus⟧.
Use of Participles.
As an Adjective the Participle may be used either as an attributive or predicate modifier of a Substantive.
1. Attributive Use. This presents no special peculiarities. Examples are:—
⟦b:glōria est cōnsentiēns laus bonōrum⟧, ⟦i:glory is the unanimous praise of the good⟧;
⟦b:Conōn mūrōs ā Lysandrō dīrutōs reficit⟧, ⟦i:Conon restored the walls destroyed by Lysander.⟧
2. Predicate Use. Here the Participle is often equivalent to a subordinate clause. Thus the Participle may denote:—
⟦i:a⟧) Time; as,—
⟦b:omne malum nāscēns facile opprimitur⟧, ⟦i:every evil is easily crushed at birth.⟧
⟦i:b⟧) A Condition; as,—
⟦b:mente ūtī nōn possumus cibō et pōtiōne complētī⟧, ⟦i:if gorged with food and drink, we cannot use our intellects⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) Manner; as,—
⟦b:Solōn senēscere sē dīcēbat multa in diēs addiscentem⟧, ⟦i:Solon said he grew old learning many new things daily.⟧
⟦i:d⟧) Means; as,—
⟦b:sōl oriēns diem cōnficit⟧, ⟦i:the sun, by its rising, makes the day.⟧
⟦i:e⟧) Opposition ('⟦i:though⟧'); as,—
⟦b:mendācī hominī nē vērum quidem dīcentī crēdimus⟧, ⟦i:we do not believe a liar, though he speaks the truth.⟧
⟦i:f⟧) Cause; as,—
⟦b:perfidiam veritus ad suōs recessit⟧, ⟦i:since he feared treachery, he returned to his own troops.⟧
3. ⟦b:Videō⟧ and ⟦b:audiō⟧, besides the Infinitive, take the Present Participle in the Predicate use; as,—
⟦b:videō tē fugientem⟧, ⟦i:I see you fleeing.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. So frequently ⟦b:faciō⟧, ⟦b:fingō⟧, ⟦b:indūcō⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; as,—
⟦b:eīs Catōnem respondentem facimus⟧, ⟦i:we represent Cato replying to them⟧;
⟦b:Homērus Laërtem colentem agrum facit⟧, ⟦i:Homer represents Laërtes tilling the field.⟧
4. The Future Active Participle (except ⟦b:futūrus⟧) is regularly confined to its use in the Periphrastic Conjugation, but in poets and later writers it is used independently, especially to denote ⟦i:purpose⟧; as,—
⟦b:vēnērunt castra oppugnātūrī⟧, ⟦i:they came to assault the camp.⟧
5. The Perfect Passive Participle is often equivalent to a coördinate clause; as,—
⟦b:urbem captam dīruit⟧, ⟦i:he captured and destroyed the city⟧ (lit. ⟦i:he destroyed the city captured⟧).
6. The Perfect Passive Participle in combination with a noun is sometimes equivalent to an abstract noun with a dependent Genitive; as,—
⟦b:post urbem conditam⟧, ⟦i:after the founding of the city⟧;
⟦b:Quīnctius dēfēnsus⟧, ⟦i:the defense of Quinctius⟧;
⟦b:quibus animus occupātus⟧, ⟦i:the preoccupation of the mind with which.⟧
7. ⟦b:Habeō⟧ sometimes takes a Perfect Passive Participle in the Predicate construction with a force not far removed from that of the Perfect or Pluperfect Indicative; as,—
⟦b:equitātus quem coāctum habēbat,⟧ ⟦i:the cavalry which he had collected.⟧
8. The Gerundive denotes ⟦i:obligation⟧, ⟦i:necessity⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧ Like other Participles it may be used either as Attributive or Predicate.
⟦i:a⟧) Less frequently as Attributive. Thus:—
⟦b:liber legendus⟧, ⟦i:a book worth reading⟧;
⟦b:lēgēs observandae⟧, ⟦i:laws deserving of observance⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) More frequently as Predicate.
1) In the Passive Periphrastic Conjugation (⟦b:amandus est⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧). In this use Intransitive Verbs can be used only impersonally, but admit their ordinary case-construction (Gen., Dat., Abl.); as,—
⟦b:veniendum est⟧, ⟦i:it is necessary to come⟧;
⟦b:oblīvīscendum est offēnsārum⟧, ⟦i:one must forget injuries⟧;
⟦b:numquam prōditōrī crēdendum est⟧, ⟦i:you must never trust a traitor⟧;
⟦b:suō cuique ūtendum est jūdiciō⟧, ⟦i:every man must use his own judgment⟧.
2) After ⟦b:cūrō⟧, ⟦i:provide for⟧; ⟦b:dō⟧, ⟦b:trādō⟧, ⟦i:give over⟧; ⟦b:relinquō⟧, ⟦i:leave⟧; ⟦b:concēdō⟧, ⟦i:hand over⟧, and some other verbs, instead of an object clause, or to denote purpose; as,—
⟦b:Caesar pontem in Ararī faciendum cūrāvit⟧, ⟦i:Caesar provided for the construction of a bridge over the Arar⟧;
⟦b:imperātor urbem mīlitibus dīripiendam concessit⟧, ⟦i:the general handed over the city to the soldiers to plunder⟧.
9. For the Gerundive as the equivalent of the Gerund, see § 339, 1.

title: The Gerund
text:
As a verbal noun the Gerund admits noun constructions as follows:—
1. ⟦b:Genitive⟧. The Genitive of the Gerund is used—
⟦i:a⟧) With Nouns, as objective or Appositional Genitive (see §§ 200, 202); as,—
⟦b:cupiditās dominandī⟧, ⟦i:desire of ruling⟧;
⟦b:ars scrībendī⟧, ⟦i:the art of writing⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) With Adjectives; as,—
⟦b:cupidus audiendī⟧, ⟦i:desirous of hearing⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) With ⟦b:causā⟧, ⟦b:grātiā⟧; as,—
⟦b:discendī causā⟧, ⟦i:for the sake of learning⟧.
2. ⟦b:Dative.⟧ The Dative of the Gerund is used—
⟦i:a⟧) With Adjectives; as,—
⟦b:aqua ūtilis est bibendō⟧, ⟦i:water is useful for drinking⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) With Verbs (rarely); as,—
⟦b:adfuī scrībendō⟧, ⟦i:I was present at the writing⟧.
3. ⟦b:Accusative⟧. The Accusative of the Gerund is used only with Prepositions, chiefly ⟦b:ad⟧ and ⟦b:in⟧ to denote purpose; as,—
⟦b:homō ad agendum nātus est⟧, ⟦i:man is born for action⟧.
4. ⟦b:Ablative⟧. The Ablative of the Gerund is used—
⟦i:a⟧) Without a Preposition, as an Ablative of Means, Cause, ⟦i:etc.⟧ (see §§ 218, 219); as,—
⟦b:mēns discendō alitur et cōgitandō⟧, ⟦i:the mind is nourished by learning and reflection⟧.
⟦b:Themistoclēs maritimōs praedōnēs cōnsectandō mare tūtum reddidit⟧, ⟦i:Themistocles made the sea safe by following up the pirates⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) After the prepositions ⟦b:ā⟧, ⟦b:dē⟧, ⟦b:ex⟧, ⟦b:in⟧; as,—
⟦b:summa voluptās ex discendō capitur⟧, ⟦i:the keenest pleasure is derived from learning⟧;
⟦b:multa dē bene beātēque vīvendō ā Platōne disputāta sunt⟧, ⟦i:there was much discussion by Plato on the subject of living well and happily⟧.
5. As a rule, only the Genitive of the Gerund and the Ablative (without a preposition) admit a Direct Object.
Gerundive Construction instead of the Gerund.
1. Instead of the Genitive or Ablative of the Gerund with a Direct Object, another construction ⟦i:may be, and very often is, used⟧. This consists in putting the Direct Object in the case of the Gerund (Gen. or Abl.) and using the Gerundive in agreement with it. This is called the Gerundive Construction. Thus:—
GERUND CONSTRUCTION.  GERUNDIVE CONSTRUCTION.
⟦b:cupidus urbem videndī⟧, ⟦i:desirous of seeing the city⟧.  ⟦b:cupidus urbis videndae⟧;
⟦b:dēlector ōrātōrēs legendō⟧, ⟦i:I am charmed with reading the orators⟧.  ⟦b:dēlector ōrātōribus legendīs⟧
⟦/⟧
2. The Gerundive Construction ⟦i:must be used⟧ to avoid a Direct Object with the Dative of the Gerund, or with a case dependent upon a Preposition; as,—
⟦b:locus castrīs mūniendīs aptus⟧, ⟦i:a place adapted to fortifying a camp⟧;
⟦b:ad pācem petendam vēnērunt⟧, ⟦i:they came to ask peace⟧;
⟦b:multum temporis cōnsūmō in legendīs poētīs⟧, ⟦i:I spend much time in reading the poets⟧.
3. In order to avoid ambiguity (see § 236, 2), the Gerundive Construction must not be employed in case of Neuter Adjectives used substantively. Thus regularly—
⟦b:philosophī cupidī sunt vērum invēstīgandī⟧, ⟦i:philosophers are eager for discovering truth⟧ (rarely ⟦b:vērī invēstīgandī⟧);
⟦b:studium plūra cognōscendī⟧, ⟦i:a desire of knowing more⟧ (not ⟦b:plūrium cognōscendōrum⟧).
4. From the nature of the case only Transitive Verbs can be used in the Gerundive construction; but ⟦b:ūtor⟧, ⟦b:fruor⟧, ⟦b:fungor⟧, ⟦b:potior⟧ (originally transitive) regularly admit it; as,—
⟦b:hostēs in spem potiundōrum castrōrum vēnerant⟧, ⟦i:the enemy had conceived the hope of gaining possession of the camp⟧.
5. The Genitives ⟦b:meī⟧, ⟦b:tuī⟧, ⟦b:suī⟧, ⟦b:nostrī⟧, ⟦b:vestrī⟧, when used in the Gerundive Construction, are regularly employed without reference to Gender or Number, since they were originally Neuter Singular Adjectives used substantively. Thus:—
⟦b:mulier suī servandī causā aufūgit⟧, ⟦i:the woman fled for the sake of saving herself⟧;
⟦b:lēgātī in castra vēnērunt suī pūrgandī causā⟧, ⟦i:the envoys came into camp for the purpose of clearing themselves⟧.
So ⟦b:nostrī servandī causā⟧, ⟦i:for the sake of saving ourselves⟧.
6. Occasionally the Genitive of the Gerundive Construction is used to denote ⟦i:purpose⟧; as,—
⟦b:quae ille cēpit lēgum ac lībertātis subvertundae⟧, ⟦i:which he undertook for the purpose of overthrowing the laws and liberty⟧.
7. The Dative of the Gerundive Construction occurs in some expressions which have the character of formulas; as,—
⟦b:decemvirī lēgibus scrībundīs⟧, ⟦i:decemvirs for codifying the laws⟧;
⟦b:quīndecimvirī sacrīs faciundīs⟧, ⟦i:quindecimvirs for performing the sacrifices⟧.

title: The Supine
text:
1. The Supine in ⟦b:-um⟧ is used after Verbs of motion to express ⟦i:purpose⟧; as,—
⟦b:lēgātī ad Caesarem grātulātum convēnērunt⟧, ⟦i:envoys came to Caesar to congratulate him⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. The Supine in ⟦b:-um⟧ may take an Object; as,—
⟦b:pācem petītum ōrātōrēs Rōmam mittunt⟧, ⟦i:they send envoys to Rome to ask for peace⟧.
⟦i:b⟧. Note the phrase:—
⟦b:dō (collocō) fīliam nūptum⟧, ⟦i:I give my daughter in marriage⟧.
2. The Supine in ⟦b:-ū⟧ is used as an Ablative of Specification with ⟦b:facilis⟧, ⟦b:difficilis⟧, ⟦b:incrēdibilis⟧, ⟦b:jūcundus⟧, ⟦b:optimus⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧; also with ⟦b:fās est⟧, ⟦b:nefās est⟧, ⟦b:opus est⟧; as,—
⟦b:haec rēs est facilis cognitū⟧, ⟦i:this thing is easy to learn⟧;
⟦b:hōc est optimum factū⟧, ⟦i:this is best to do⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Only a few Supines in ⟦b:-ū⟧ are in common use, chiefly ⟦b:audītū⟧, ⟦b:cognitū⟧, ⟦b:dictū⟧, ⟦b:factū⟧, ⟦b:vīsū⟧.
⟦i:b⟧. The Supine in ⟦b:-ū⟧ never takes an Object.

title: Coördinate Conjunctions
text:
⟦b:Copulative Conjunctions.⟧ These ⟦i:join⟧ one word, phrase, or clause to another.
1.
⟦i:a⟧) ⟦b:et⟧ simply connects.
⟦i:b⟧) ⟦b:-que⟧ joins more closely than ⟦b:et⟧, and is used especially where the two members have an internal connection with each other; as,—
⟦b:parentēs līberīque⟧, ⟦i:parents and children⟧;
⟦b:cum hominēs aestū febrīque jactantur⟧, ⟦i:when people are tossed about with heat and fever⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) ⟦b:atque⟧ (⟦b:ac⟧) usually emphasizes the second of the two things connected,—⟦i:and also, and indeed, and in fact⟧. After words of ⟦i:likeness⟧ and ⟦i:difference⟧, ⟦b:atque⟧ (⟦b:ac⟧) has the force of ⟦i:as⟧, ⟦i:than⟧. Thus:—
⟦b:ego idem sentiō ac tū⟧, ⟦i:I think the same as you⟧;
⟦b:haud aliter ac⟧, ⟦i:not otherwise than⟧.
⟦i:d⟧) ⟦b:neque⟧ (⟦b:nec⟧) means ⟦i:and not⟧, ⟦i:neither⟧, ⟦i:nor⟧.
2.
⟦i:a⟧) ⟦b:-que⟧ is an enclitic, and is appended always to the second of two words connected. Where it connects phrases or clauses, it is appended to the first word of the second clause; but when the first word of the second clause is a Preposition, ⟦b:-que⟧ is regularly appended to the next following word; as,—
⟦b:ob eamque rem⟧, ⟦i:and on account of that thing⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) ⟦b:atque⟧ is used before vowels and consonants; ⟦b:ac⟧ never before vowels, and seldom before ⟦b:c⟧, ⟦b:g⟧, ⟦b:qu⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) ⟦b:et nōn⟧ is used for ⟦b:neque⟧ when the emphasis of the negative rests upon a special word; as,—
⟦b:vetus et nōn ignōbilis ōrātor⟧, ⟦i:an old and not ignoble orator⟧.
⟦i:d⟧) For ⟦i:and nowhere⟧, ⟦i:and never⟧, ⟦i:and none⟧, the Latin regularly said ⟦b:nec ūsquam⟧, ⟦b:nec umquam⟧, ⟦b:nec ūllus⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧
3. ⟦b:Correlatives.⟧ Copulative Conjunctions are frequently used correlatively; as,—
⟦b:et ... et⟧, ⟦i:both ... and⟧;
⟦b:neque (nec) ... neque (nec)⟧, ⟦i:neither ... nor⟧;
⟦b:cum ... tum⟧, ⟦i:while ... at the same time⟧;
⟦b:tum ... tum⟧, ⟦i:not only ... but also⟧.
Less frequently:—
⟦b:et ... neque⟧; ⟦b:neque ... et⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Note that the Latin, with its tendency to emphasize antithetical relations, often uses correlatives, especially ⟦b:et ... et⟧, ⟦b:et ... neque⟧, ⟦b:neque ... et⟧, where the English employs but a single connective.
4. ⟦b:In enumerations⟧—
⟦i:a⟧) The different members of a series may follow one another without connectives (Asyndeton; see § 346). Thus:—
⟦b:ex cupiditātibus odia, discidia, discordiae, sēditiōnēs, bella nāscuntur⟧, ⟦i:from covetous desires spring up hatred, dissension, discord, sedition, wars⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) The different members may severally be connected by ⟦b:et⟧ (Polysyndeton). Thus:—
⟦b:hōrae cēdunt et diēs et mēnsēs et annī⟧, ⟦i:hours and days and months and years pass away⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) The connective may be omitted between the former members, while the last two are connected by ⟦b:-que⟧ (rarely ⟦b:et⟧); as,—
⟦b:Caesar in Carnutēs, Andēs Turonēsque legiōnēs dēdūcit⟧, ⟦i:Caesar leads his legions into the territory of the Carnutes, Andes, and Turones⟧.
⟦b:Disjunctive Conjunctions⟧ indicate an ⟦i:alternative⟧.
1.
⟦i:a⟧) aut must be used when the alternatives are mutually exclusive; as,—
⟦b:cita mors venit aut victōria laeta⟧, ⟦i:(either) swift death or glad victory comes⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) ⟦b:vel⟧, ⟦b:-ve⟧ (enclitic) imply a choice between the alternatives; as,—
⟦b:quī aethēr vel caelum nōminātur⟧, ⟦i:which is called aether or heaven⟧.
2. ⟦b:Correlatives⟧. Disjunctive Conjunctions are often used correlatively; as,—
⟦b:aut ... aut⟧, ⟦i:either ... or⟧;
⟦b:vel ... vel⟧, ⟦i:either ... or⟧;
⟦b:sīve ... sīve⟧, ⟦i:if ... or if⟧.
⟦b:Adversative Conjunctions.⟧ These denote ⟦i:opposition⟧.
1.
⟦i:a⟧) ⟦b:sed⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, merely denotes opposition.
⟦i:b⟧) ⟦b:vērum⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, is stronger than ⟦b:sed⟧, but is less frequently used.
⟦i:c⟧) ⟦b:autem⟧, ⟦i:but on the other hand⟧, ⟦i:however⟧, marks a transition. It is always post-positive.
DEFINITION. A post-positive word is one that cannot begin a sentence, but is placed after one or more words.
⟦i:d⟧) ⟦b:at⟧, ⟦i:but⟧, is used especially in disputation, to introduce an opposing argument.
⟦i:e⟧) ⟦b:atquī⟧ means ⟦i:but yet⟧.
⟦i:f⟧) ⟦b:tamen⟧, ⟦i:yet⟧, usually stands after the emphatic word, but not always.
⟦i:g⟧) ⟦b:vērō⟧, ⟦i:however⟧, ⟦i:indeed⟧, ⟦i:in truth⟧, is always post-positive.
2. Note the correlative expressions:—
⟦b:nōn sōlum (nōn modo) ... sed etiam⟧, ⟦i:not only ... but also⟧;
⟦b:nōn modo nōn ... sed nē ... quidem⟧, ⟦i:not only not, but not even⟧; as,—
⟦b:nōn modo tibi nōn īrāscor, sed nē reprehendō quidem factum tuum⟧, ⟦i:I not only am not angry with you, but I do not even blame your action⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. But when the sentence has but one verb, and this stands with the second member, ⟦b:nōn modo⟧ may be used for ⟦b:nōn modo nōn⟧; as,—
⟦b:adsentātiō nōn modo amīcō, sed nē līberō quidem digne est⟧, ⟦i:flattery is not only not worthy of a friend, but not even of a free man.⟧
⟦b:Illative Conjunctions⟧. These represent the statement which they introduce as ⟦i:following from⟧ or as ⟦i:in conformity with⟧ what has preceded.
1.
⟦i:a⟧) ⟦b:itaque⟧ = ⟦i:and so⟧, ⟦i:accordingly⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) ⟦b:ergō⟧ = ⟦i:therefore⟧, ⟦i:accordingly⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) ⟦b:igitur⟧ (regularly post-positive) = ⟦i:therefore⟧, ⟦i:accordingly⟧.
2. ⟦b:Igitur⟧ is never combined with ⟦b:et⟧, ⟦b:atque⟧, ⟦b:-que⟧, or ⟦b:neque⟧.
⟦b:Causal Conjunctions⟧. These denote ⟦i:cause⟧, or ⟦i:give an explanation⟧. They are ⟦b:nam⟧, ⟦b:namque⟧, ⟦b:enim⟧ (post-positive), ⟦b:etenim⟧, ⟦i:for⟧.
⟦b:Asyndeton⟧. The conjunction is sometimes omitted between coördinate members, particularly in lively or impassioned narration. Thus:—
⟦i:a⟧) A copulative Conjunction is omitted; as,—
⟦b:avāritia īnfīnīta, īnsatiābilis est⟧, ⟦i:avarice is boundless (and) insatiable⟧;
⟦b:Cn. Pompejō, M. Crassō cōnsulibus⟧, ⟦i:in the consulship of Gnaeus Pompey (and) Marcus Crassus⟧.
The conjunction is regularly omitted between the names of consuls when the praenomen (⟦i:Mārcus⟧, ⟦i:Gaius⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧) is expressed.
⟦i:b⟧) An Adversative Conjunction may be omitted; as,—
⟦b:ratiōnēs dēfuērunt, ūbertās ōrātiōnis nōn dēfuit⟧, ⟦i:arguments were lacking, (but) abundance of words was not⟧.

title: Syntax of adverbs
text:
1. The following particles, sometimes classed as Conjunctions, are more properly Adverbs:—
⟦b:etiam⟧, ⟦i:also⟧, ⟦i:even⟧.
⟦b:quoque⟧ (always post-positive), ⟦i:also⟧.
⟦b:quidem⟧ (always post-positive) lays stress upon the preceding word. It is sometimes equivalent to the English ⟦i:indeed⟧, ⟦i:in fact⟧, but more frequently cannot be rendered, except by vocal emphasis.
⟦b:nē ... quidem⟧ means ⟦i:not even⟧; the emphatic word or phrase always stands between; as, ⟦b:nē ille quidem⟧, ⟦i:not even he⟧.
⟦b:tamen⟧ and ⟦b:vērō⟧, in addition to their use as Conjunctions, are often employed as Adverbs.
2. ⟦b:Negatives.⟧ Two negatives are regularly equivalent to an affirmative as in English, as ⟦b:nōn nūllī⟧, ⟦i:some⟧; but when ⟦b:nōn⟧, ⟦b:nēmō⟧, ⟦b:nihil⟧, ⟦b:numquam⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧, are accompanied by ⟦b:neque ... neque⟧, ⟦b:nōn ... nōn⟧, ⟦b:nōn modo⟧, or ⟦b:nē ... quidem⟧, the latter particles simply take up the negation and emphasize it; as,—
⟦b:habeō hīc nēminem neque amīcum neque cognātum⟧, ⟦i:I have here no one, neither friend nor relative⟧.
⟦b:nōn enim praetereundum est nē id quidem⟧, ⟦i:for not even that must be passed by.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. ⟦b:Haud⟧ in Cicero and Caesar occurs almost exclusively as a modifier of Adjectives and Adverbs, and in the phrase ⟦b:haud sciō an⟧. Later writers use it freely with verbs.

title: Word-order
text:
In the normal arrangement of the Latin sentence the Subject stands at the beginning of the sentence, the Predicate at the end; as,—
⟦b:Dārīus classem quīngentārum nāvium comparāvit⟧, ⟦i:Darius got ready a fleet of five hundred ships⟧.
But for the sake of emphasis the normal arrangement is often abandoned, and the emphatic word is put at the beginning, less frequently at the end of the sentence; as,—
⟦b:magnus in hōc bellō Themistoclēs fuit⟧, GREAT ⟦i:was Themistocles in this war⟧;
⟦b:aliud iter habēmus nūllum⟧, ⟦i:other course we have⟧ NONE.

title: Word-order: special principles
text:
1. ⟦b:Nouns.⟧ A Genitive or other oblique case regularly follows the word upon which it depends. Thus:—
⟦i:a⟧) Depending upon a Noun:—
⟦b:tribūnus plēbis⟧, ⟦i:tribune of the plebs⟧;
⟦b:fīlius rēgis⟧, ⟦i:son of the king⟧;
⟦b:vir magnī animī⟧, ⟦i:a man of noble spirit⟧.
Yet always ⟦b:senātūs cōnsultum⟧, ⟦b:plēbis scītum⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) Depending upon an Adjective:—
⟦b:ignārus rērum⟧, ⟦i:ignorant of affairs⟧;
⟦b:dignī amīcitiā⟧, ⟦i:worthy of friendship⟧;
⟦b:plūs aequō⟧, ⟦i:more than (what is) fair⟧.
2. ⟦b:Appositives.⟧ An Appositive regularly follows its Subject; as,—
⟦b:Philippus, rēx Macedonum⟧, ⟦i:Philip, king of the Macedonians⟧;
⟦b:adsentātiō, vitiōrum adjūtrīx⟧, ⟦i:flattery, promoter of evils⟧.
Yet ⟦b:flūmen Rhēnus⟧, ⟦i:the River Rhine⟧; and always in good prose ⟦b:urbs Rōma⟧, ⟦i:the city Rome⟧.
3. The ⟦b:Vocative⟧ usually follows one or more words; as,—
⟦b:audī, Caesar⟧, ⟦i:hear, Caesar!⟧
4. ⟦b:Adjectives.⟧ No general law can be laid down for the position of Adjectives. On the whole they precede the noun oftener than they follow it.
⟦i:a⟧. Adjectives of ⟦i:quantity⟧ (including ⟦i:numerals⟧) regularly precede their noun; as,—
⟦b:omnēs hominēs⟧, ⟦i:all men⟧;
⟦b:septingentae nāvēs⟧, ⟦i:seven hundred vessels⟧.
⟦i:b⟧. Note the force of position in the following:—
⟦b:media urbs⟧, ⟦i:the middle of the city⟧;
⟦b:urbs media⟧, ⟦i:the middle city⟧,
⟦b:extrēmum bellum⟧, ⟦i:the end of the war⟧;
⟦b:bellum extrēmum⟧, ⟦i:the last war⟧.
⟦i:c⟧. ⟦b:Rōmānus⟧ and ⟦b:Latīnus⟧ regularly follow; as,—
⟦b:senātus populusque Rōmānus⟧, ⟦i:the Roman Senate and People⟧;
⟦b:lūdī Rōmānī⟧, ⟦i:the Roman games⟧;
⟦b:fēriae Latīnae⟧, ⟦i:the Latin holidays⟧.
⟦i:d⟧. When a Noun is modified both by an Adjective and by a Genitive, a favorite order is: Adjective, Genitive, Noun; as,—
⟦b:summa omnium rērum abundantia⟧, ⟦i:the greatest abundance of all things⟧.
5. ⟦b:Pronouns.⟧
⟦i:a⟧. The Demonstrative, Relative, and Interrogative Pronouns regularly precede the Noun; as,—
⟦b:hīc homō⟧, ⟦i:this man⟧;
⟦b:ille homō⟧, ⟦i:that man⟧;
⟦b:erant duo itinera, quibus itineribus⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧, ⟦i:there were two routes, by which⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧
⟦b:quī homō⟧? ⟦i:what sort of man⟧?
⟦i:b⟧. But ⟦b:ille⟧ in the sense of '⟦i:that well known⟧,' '⟦i:that famous⟧,' usually stands after its Noun; as,—
⟦b:testula illa⟧, ⟦i:that well-known custom of ostracism⟧;
⟦b:Mēdēa illa⟧, ⟦i:that famous Medea⟧.
⟦i:c⟧. Possessive and Indefinite Pronouns usually follow their Noun; as,—
⟦b:pater meus⟧, ⟦i:my father⟧;
⟦b:homō quīdam⟧, ⟦i:a certain man⟧;
⟦b:mulier aliqua⟧, ⟦i:some woman⟧.
But for purposes of contrast the Possessive often precedes its Noun; as,—
⟦b:meus pater⟧, MY ⟦i:father⟧ (⟦i:i.e.⟧ as opposed to ⟦i:yours⟧, ⟦i:his⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧).
⟦i:d⟧. Where two or more Pronouns occur in the same sentence, the Latin is fond of putting them in close proximity; as,—
⟦b:nisi forte ego vōbīs cessāre videor⟧, ⟦i:unless perchance I seem to you to be doing nothing⟧.
6. Adverbs and Adverbial phrases regularly precede the word they modify; as,—
⟦b:valdē dīligēns⟧, ⟦i:extremely diligent⟧;
⟦b:saepe dīxī⟧, ⟦i:I have often said⟧;
⟦b:tē jam diū hortāmur⟧, ⟦i:we have long been urging you⟧;
⟦b:paulō post⟧, ⟦i:a little after⟧.
7. ⟦b:Prepositions⟧ regularly precede the words they govern.
⟦i:a⟧. But limiting words often intervene between the Preposition and its case; as,—
⟦b:dē commūnī hominum memoriā⟧, ⟦i:concerning the common memory of men⟧;
⟦b:ad beātē vīvendum⟧, ⟦i:for living happily⟧.
⟦i:b⟧. When a noun is modified by an Adjective, the Adjective is often placed before the preposition; as,—
⟦b:magnō in dolōre⟧, ⟦i:in great grief⟧;
⟦b:summā cum laude⟧, ⟦i:with the highest credit⟧;
⟦b:quā dē causā⟧, ⟦i:for which cause⟧;
⟦b:hanc ob rem⟧, ⟦i:on account of this thing⟧.
⟦i:c⟧. For Anastrophe, by which a Preposition is put after its case, see § 144, 3.
8. ⟦b:Conjunctions. Autem⟧, ⟦b:enim⟧, and ⟦b:igitur⟧ regularly stand in the second place in the sentence, but when combined with ⟦b:est⟧ or ⟦b:sunt⟧ they often stand third; as,—
⟦b:ita est enim⟧, ⟦i:for so it is⟧.
9. Words or Phrases referring to the preceding sentence or to some part of it, regularly stand first; as,—
⟦b:id ut audīvit, Corcyram dēmigrāvit⟧, ⟦i:when he heard that⟧ (referring to the contents of the preceding sentence), ⟦i:he moved to Corcyra⟧;
⟦b:eō cum Caesar vēnisset, timentēs cōnfirmat⟧, ⟦i:when Caesar had come thither⟧ (⟦i:i.e.⟧ to the place just mentioned), ⟦i:he encouraged the timid⟧.
10. The Latin has a fondness for putting side by side words which are etymologically related; as,—
⟦b:ut ad senem senex dē senectūte, sīc hōc librō ad amīcum amīcissimus dē amīcitiā scrīpsī⟧, ⟦i:as I, an old man, wrote to an old man, on old age, so in this book, as a fond friend, I have written to a friend, concerning friendship⟧.
11. Special rhetorical devices for indicating emphasis are the following:—
⟦i:a⟧) ⟦b:Hypérbaton⟧, which consists in the separation of words that regularly stand together; as,—
⟦b:septimus mihi Orīginum liber est in manibus⟧, ⟦i:the seventh book of my 'Origines' is under way⟧;
⟦b:receptō Caesar Ōricō proficīscitur⟧, ⟦i:having recovered Oricus, Caesar set out⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) ⟦b:Anáphora⟧, which consists in the repetition of the same word or the same word-order in successive phrases; as,—
⟦b:sed plēnī omnēs sunt librī, plēnae sapientium vōcēs, plēna exemplōrum vetustās⟧, ⟦i:but all books are full of it, the voices of sages are full of it, antiquity is full of examples of it⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) ⟦b:Chiásmus⟧, which consists in changing the relative order of words in two antithetical phrases; as,—
⟦b:multōs dēfendī, laesī nēminem⟧, ⟦i:many have I defended, I have injured no one⟧;
⟦b:horribilem illum diem aliīs, nōbīs faustum⟧, ⟦i:that day dreadful to others, for us fortunate⟧.
⟦i:d⟧) ⟦b:Sýnchysis⟧, or the interlocked arrangement. This is mostly confined to poetry, yet occurs in rhetorical prose, especially that of the Imperial Period; as,—
⟦b:simulātam Pompejānārum grātiam partium⟧, ⟦i:pretended interest in the Pompeian party⟧.
12. ⟦b:Metrical Close⟧. At the end of a sentence certain cadences were avoided; others were much employed. Thus:—
⟦i:a⟧) Cadences avoided.
as, ⟦b:esse vidētur⟧ (close of hexameter).
as, ⟦b:esse potest⟧ (close of pentameter).
⟦i:b⟧) Cadences frequently employed.
as, ⟦b:auxerant⟧.
as, ⟦b:comprobāvit⟧.
as, ⟦b:esse videātur⟧.
as, ⟦b:rogātū tuō⟧.

title: Sentence-structure
text:
1. ⟦b:Unity of Subject.⟧—In complex sentences the Latin regularly holds to unity of Subject in the different members; as,—
⟦b:Caesar prīmum suō, deinde omnium ex cōnspectū remōtīs equīs, ut aequātō perīculō spem fugae tolleret, cohortātus suōs proelium commīsit⟧, ⟦i:Caesar having first removed his own horse from sight, then the horses of all, in order, by making the danger equal, to take away hope of flight, encouraged his men and joined battle⟧.
2. A word serving as the common Subject or Object of the main clause and a subordinate one, stands before both; as,—
⟦b:Haeduī cum sē dēfendere nōn possent, lēgātōs ad Caesarem mittunt⟧, ⟦i:since the Haedui could not defend themselves, they sent envoys to Caesar⟧;
⟦b:ille etsī flagrābat bellandī cupiditāte, tamen pācī serviendum putāvit⟧, ⟦i:although he was burning with a desire to fight, yet he thought he ought to aim at peace⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. The same is true also
1) When the Subject of the main clause is Object (Direct or Indirect) of a subordinate clause; as,—
⟦b:Caesar, cum hōc eī nūntiatum esset, mātūrat ab urbe proficīscī⟧, ⟦i:when this had been reported to Caesar he hastened to set out from the city⟧.
2) When the Subject of a subordinate clause is at the same time the Object (Direct or Indirect) of the main clause; as,—
⟦b:L. Mānliō, cum dictātor fuisset, M. Pompōnius tribūnus plēbis diem dīxit⟧, ⟦i:M. Pomponius, tribune of the people, instituted proceedings against Lucius Manlius, though he had been dictator⟧.
3. Of subordinate clauses, temporal, conditional, and adversative clauses more commonly precede the main clause; indirect questions and clauses of purpose or result more commonly follow; as,—
⟦b:postquam haec dīxit, profectus est⟧, ⟦i:after he said this, he set out⟧;
⟦b:sī quis ita agat, imprūdēns sit⟧, ⟦i:if any one should act so, he would be devoid of foresight⟧;
⟦b:accidit ut ūnā nocte omnēs Hermae dēicerentur⟧, ⟦i:it happened that in a single night all the Hermae were thrown down⟧.
4. Sometimes in Latin the main verb is placed within the subordinate clause; as,—
⟦b:sī quid est in mē ingenī, quod sentiō quam sit exiguum⟧, ⟦i:if there is any talent in me, and I know how little it is⟧.
5. ⟦b:The Latin Period.⟧ The term Period, when strictly used, designates a compound sentence in which the subordinate clauses are inserted within the main clause; as,—
⟦b:Caesar etsī intellegēbat quā dē causā ea dīcerentur, tamen, nē aestātem in Trēverīs cōnsūmere cōgerētur, Indutiomārum ad sē venīre jussit⟧, ⟦i:though Caesar perceived why this was said, yet, lest he should be forced to spend the summer among the Treveri, he ordered Indutiomarus to come to him⟧.
In the Periodic structure the thought is suspended until the end of the sentence is reached. Many Roman writers were extremely fond of this sentence-structure, and it was well adapted to the inflectional character of their language; in English we generally avoid it.
6. When there are several subordinate clauses in one Period, the Latin so arranges them as to avoid a succession of verbs. Thus:—
⟦b:At hostēs cum mīsissent, quī, quae in castrīs gererentur, cognōscerent, ubi sē dēceptōs intellēxērunt, omnibus cōpiīs subsecūtī ad flūmen contendunt⟧, ⟦i:but the enemy when they had sent men to learn what was going on in camp, after discovering that they had been outwitted, followed with all their forces and hurried to the river⟧.
In this chapter brief consideration is given to a few features of Latin diction which belong rather to style than to formal grammar.

title: Style: nouns
Style: adjectives
Style: pronouns
text:
1. In Compound Sentences the Relative Pronoun has a fondness for connecting itself with the subordinate clause rather than the main one; as,—
⟦b:ā quō cum quaererētur, quid maximē expedīret, respondit⟧, ⟦i:when it was asked of him what was best, he replied⟧. (Less commonly, ⟦b:quī, cum ab eō quaererētur, respondit⟧.)
2. ⟦b:Uterque⟧, ⟦b:ambō⟧. ⟦b:Uterque⟧ means ⟦i:each of two⟧; ⟦b:ambō⟧ means ⟦i:both⟧; as,—
⟦b:uterque frāter abiit⟧, ⟦i:each of the two brothers departed⟧ (⟦i:i.e.⟧ separately);
⟦b:ambō frātrēs abiērunt⟧, ⟦i:i.e.⟧ the two brothers departed together.
⟦i:a⟧. The Plural of ⟦b:uterque⟧ occurs—
1) With Nouns used only in the Plural (see § 56); as,—
⟦b:in utrīsque castrīs⟧, ⟦i:in each camp⟧.
2) Where there is a distinct reference to two groups of persons or things; as,—
⟦b:utrīque ducēs clārī fuērunt⟧, ⟦i:the generals on each side⟧ (several in number) ⟦i:were famous⟧.

title: Style: verbs
Peculiarities in the Use of the Accusative
Peculiarities in Connection with the Use of the Dative
text:
1. The English ⟦i:for⟧ does not always correspond to a Dative notion in Latin, but is often the equivalent of ⟦b:prō⟧ with the Ablative, ⟦i:viz.⟧ in the senses—
⟦i:a⟧) ⟦i:In defense of⟧; as,—
⟦b:prō patriā morī⟧, ⟦i:to die for one's country⟧.
⟦i:b⟧) ⟦i:Instead of⟧, ⟦i:in behalf of⟧; as,—
⟦b:ūnus prō omnibus dīxit⟧, ⟦i:one spoke for all⟧;
⟦b:haec prō lēge dicta sunt⟧, ⟦i:these things were said for the law⟧.
⟦i:c⟧) ⟦i:In proportion to⟧; as,—
⟦b:prō multitūdine hominum eōrum fīnēs erant angustī⟧, ⟦i:for the population, their territory was small⟧.
2. Similarly, English ⟦i:to⟧ when it indicates motion is rendered in Latin by ⟦b:ad⟧.
⟦i:a⟧. Note, however, that the Latin may say either ⟦b:scrībere ad aliquem⟧, or ⟦b:scrībere alicui⟧, according as the idea of motion is or is not predominant. So in several similar expressions.
3. In the poets, verbs of ⟦i:mingling with⟧, ⟦i:contending with⟧, ⟦i:joining⟧, ⟦i:clinging to⟧, ⟦i:etc.⟧, sometimes take the Dative. This construction is a Grecism. Thus:—
⟦b:sē miscet virīs⟧, ⟦i:he mingles with the men⟧;
⟦b:contendis Homērō⟧, ⟦i:you contend with Homer⟧;
⟦b:dextrae dextram jungere⟧, ⟦i:to clasp hand with hand⟧.

title: Peculiarities in the Use of the Genitive
text:
1. The Possessive Genitive gives emphasis to the ⟦i:possessor⟧, the Dative of Possessor emphasizes ⟦i:the fact of possession⟧; as,—
⟦b:hortus patris est⟧, ⟦i:the garden is my father's⟧;
⟦b:mihi hortus est⟧, ⟦i:I possess a garden⟧.
2. The Latin can say either ⟦b:stultī⟧ or ⟦b:stultum est dīcere⟧, ⟦i:it is foolish to say⟧; but Adjectives of one ending permit only the Genitive; as,—
⟦b:sapientis est haec sēcum reputāre⟧, ⟦i:it is the part of a wise man to consider this⟧.
